title: Chapter 30. Of the Office of the Sovereign Representative
paragraphs: The OFFICE of the sovereign (whether monarch or assembly) consists in the end for which he was entrusted with the sovereign power — namely, the procuring of the safety of the people, to which he is obliged by the law of nature, and is to render account of it to God, the author of that law, and to no one else. By 'safety' here is meant not a bare preservation, but also all the other contentments of life which every man, by lawful industry, without danger or hurt to the commonwealth, shall acquire for himself.

This is intended to be done not by care applied to individuals (beyond their protection from injuries when they shall complain), but by a general providence contained in public instruction, both of doctrine and example, and in the making and executing of good laws, to which individual persons may apply their own cases.
It is against the duty of a sovereign to relinquish any essential right of sovereignty, or to fail to see the people taught the grounds of them.

Because, if the essential rights of sovereignty (specified before in the eighteenth chapter) are taken away, the commonwealth is thereby dissolved, and every man returns into the condition and calamity of a war with every other man (which is the greatest evil that can happen in this life), it is the office of the sovereign to maintain those rights entire; and consequently it is against his duty, first, to transfer to another, or to lay aside, any of them. For he who deserts the means deserts the end; and he deserts the means who, being the sovereign, acknowledges himself subject to the civil laws, and renounces the power of supreme judicature, or of making war or peace by his own authority, or of judging of the necessities of the commonwealth, or of levying money and soldiers when and as much as in his own conscience he shall judge necessary, or of making officers and ministers both of war and peace, or of appointing teachers and examining what doctrines are conformable, or contrary, to the defence, peace, and good of the people. Second, it is against his duty to let the people be ignorant, or misinformed, of the grounds and reasons of those essential rights of his; because thereby men are easily seduced and drawn to resist him when the commonwealth shall require the use and exercise of those rights.

And the grounds of these rights have all the more need to be diligently and truly taught because they cannot be maintained by any civil law, or by the terror of legal punishment. For a civil law that forbids rebellion (and such is all resistance to the essential rights of sovereignty) is, as civil law, no obligation, but only by virtue of the law of nature, which forbids the violation of faith; and if men do not know this natural obligation, they cannot know the right of any law the sovereign makes. As for the punishment, they take it only for an act of hostility, which, when they think they have strength enough, they will try by acts of hostility to avoid.
An objection from those who say there are no principles of reason for absolute sovereignty.

As I have heard some say that justice is but a word without substance, and that whatever a man can by force or by craft acquire to himself (not only in the condition of war, but also in a commonwealth) is his own — which I have already shown to be false — so there are also those who maintain that there are no grounds or principles of reason to support those essential rights which make sovereignty absolute. For if there were, they would (these men say) have been found out in some place or other; whereas we see that until now there has been no commonwealth in which those rights have been acknowledged or claimed. In this they argue as badly as if the savage people of America were to deny that there were any grounds, or principles, of reason for building a house so as to last as long as the materials, because they have never yet seen any so well built. Time and industry produce every day new knowledge. And as the art of building well is derived from principles of reason discovered by industrious men who had long studied the nature of materials and the various effects of figure and proportion — long after mankind first began (though poorly) to build — so, long after men have begun to constitute commonwealths (imperfect, and apt to relapse into disorder), principles of reason may be found by industrious meditation. Whether men make use of them, or neglect them, concerns my own particular interest, at this day, very little. But supposing my principles are not such principles of reason, I am at least sure that they are principles from the authority of Scripture, as I shall make appear when I come to speak of the Kingdom of God (administered by Moses) over the Jews, his peculiar people by covenant.

But they say again that, though the principles are right, common people are not capable enough to be made to understand them. I should be glad if the rich and powerful subjects of a kingdom, or those reckoned the most learned, were no less incapable than the common people. But all men know that the obstacles to this kind of doctrine proceed not so much from the difficulty of the matter as from the interest of those who are to learn. Powerful men hardly digest anything that sets up a power to bridle their affections; and learned men, anything that exposes their errors, and thereby lessens their authority. Whereas the minds of common people, unless they are tainted by dependence on the powerful, or scribbled over with the opinions of their doctors, are like clean paper, fit to receive whatever is imprinted on them by public authority. Shall whole nations be brought to acquiesce in the great mysteries of the Christian religion, which are above reason, and millions of men be made to believe that the same body may be in innumerable places at one and the same time (which is against reason); and shall men not be able, by their teaching and preaching, protected by the law, to make accepted what is so consonant to reason that any unprejudiced man needs no more to learn it than to hear it? I conclude therefore that in the instruction of the people in the essential rights (which are the natural and fundamental laws) of sovereignty, there is no difficulty (so long as a sovereign has his power entire) except what proceeds from his own fault, or the fault of those he trusts in the administration of the commonwealth; and consequently it is his duty to cause them to be so instructed; and not only his duty, but also his benefit and security, against the danger that may arise to himself in his natural person from rebellion.

And (to descend to particulars) the people are to be taught: first, that they ought not to be in love with any form of government they see in their neighbour nations more than with their own; nor (whatever present prosperity they behold in nations governed otherwise than they) to desire change. For the prosperity of a people ruled by an aristocratic or democratic assembly comes not from aristocracy nor from democracy, but from the obedience and concord of the subjects; nor does a people flourish in a monarchy because one man has the right to rule them, but because they obey him. Take away in any kind of state obedience (and consequently the concord of the people), and they shall not only not flourish, but in a short time will be dissolved. And those who, by disobedience, set out to do no more than reform the commonwealth shall find that they thereby destroy it — like the foolish daughters of Pelias in the fable, who, desiring to renew the youth of their decrepit father, did, on the counsel of Medea, cut him in pieces and boil him with strange herbs, but made no new man of him. This desire of change is like the breach of the first of God's commandments: for there God says, Non Habebis Deos Alienos — 'Thou shalt not have the gods of other nations'; and in another place, concerning kings, that they are gods.

Second, they are to be taught that they ought not to be carried away by admiration for the virtue of any of their fellow subjects, however high he stands or however conspicuously he shines in the commonwealth, nor of any assembly (except the sovereign assembly), so as to defer to them any obedience or honour that belongs only to the sovereign (whom in their particular stations they represent); nor to receive any influence from them but such as is conveyed by them from the sovereign authority. For a sovereign cannot be imagined to love his people as he ought who is not jealous of them, but suffers them, by the flattery of popular men, to be seduced from their loyalty — as they have often been, not only secretly but openly, so as to have marriage with them proclaimed In Facie Ecclesiae by preachers, and the same published in the open streets — which may fitly be compared to the violation of the second of the Ten Commandments.

Third, in consequence of this, they ought to be informed how great a fault it is to speak evil of the sovereign representative (whether one man or an assembly of men), or to argue and dispute his power, or in any way to use his name irreverently, by which he may be brought into contempt with his people, and their obedience (in which the safety of the commonwealth consists) slackened. This doctrine the third commandment, by resemblance, points to.

Fourth, since the people cannot be taught this — nor, when it is taught, remember it; nor, after one generation has passed, so much as know in whom the sovereign power is placed — without setting apart from their ordinary labour certain times in which they may attend those appointed to instruct them, it is necessary that some such times be appointed, in which they may assemble together and (after prayers and praises given to God, the sovereign of sovereigns) hear those duties told to them, and the positive laws (such as generally concern them all) read and expounded, and be reminded of the authority that makes them laws. To this end the Jews had, every seventh day, a Sabbath, on which the law was read and expounded; and in the solemnity of which they were reminded that their king was God; that having created the world in six days, he rested the seventh day; and by their resting on it from their labour, that the God who had redeemed them from their servile and painful labour in Egypt was their king, and gave them a time, after they had rejoiced in God, to take joy also in themselves, by lawful recreation. So the first table of the commandments is all spent in setting down the sum of God's absolute power, not only as God but as king (by particular pact) of the Jews; and it may therefore shed light, for those to whom the sovereign power has been conferred by the consent of men, on what doctrine they ought to teach their subjects.

And because the first instruction of children depends on the care of their parents, it is necessary that children should be obedient to them while they are under their tutelage — and not only so, but also that afterwards (as gratitude requires) they acknowledge the benefit of their education by external signs of honour. To this end they are to be taught that originally the father of every man was also his sovereign lord, with power over him of life and death; and that the fathers of families, when by instituting a commonwealth they resigned that absolute power, never intended to lose the honour due to them for their education. For to relinquish such a right was not necessary for the institution of sovereign power; nor would there be any reason why a man should want to have children, or take the care to nourish and instruct them, if afterwards he were to have no other benefit from them than from other men. And this accords with the fifth commandment.

Again, every sovereign ought to cause justice to be taught — which (consisting in taking from no man what is his) is as much as to say, to cause men to be taught not to deprive their neighbour, by violence or fraud, of any thing which by the sovereign authority is theirs. Of things held in property, those dearest to a man are his own life and limbs; and in the next degree (in most men), those that concern conjugal affection; and after them, riches and means of living. Therefore the people are to be taught to abstain from violence to one another's person by private revenges; from violation of conjugal honour; and from forcible rapine and fraudulent surreption of one another's goods. For which purpose, also, it is necessary they be shown the evil consequences of false judgement, through corruption of either judges or witnesses — whereby the distinction of property is taken away, and justice becomes of no effect. All of which things are intimated in the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth commandments.

Lastly, they are to be taught that not only the unjust acts, but also the designs and intentions to do them (even when by accident hindered), are injustice; for injustice consists in the depravity of the will as well as in the irregularity of the act. And this is the intent of the tenth commandment, and the sum of the second table; which is reduced all to this one commandment of mutual charity, 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself' — as the sum of the first table is reduced to 'the love of God,' whom they had then newly received as their king.

As for the means and conduits by which the people may receive this instruction, we should ask by what means so many opinions, contrary to the peace of mankind, founded on weak and false principles, have nevertheless been so deeply rooted in them. I mean those opinions which I specified in the previous chapter: that men shall judge what is lawful and unlawful, not by the law itself, but by their own private judgements; that subjects sin in obeying the commands of the commonwealth, unless they themselves have first judged them to be lawful; that their property in their riches is such as to exclude the dominion which the commonwealth has over the same; that it is lawful for subjects to kill those they call tyrants; that the sovereign power may be divided; and the like. These come to be instilled into the people by this means. Those whom necessity or covetousness keeps intent on their trades and labour, and those, on the other hand, whom superfluity or sloth carries after their sensual pleasures (the two sorts who make up the greatest part of mankind), being diverted from the deep meditation which the learning of truth — not only in the matter of natural justice, but also of all other sciences — necessarily requires, receive the notions of their duty chiefly from divines in the pulpit, and partly from such of their neighbours, or familiar acquaintances, as, having the faculty of discoursing readily and plausibly, seem wiser and better learned in cases of law and conscience than themselves. And the divines, and others who make a show of learning, derive their knowledge from the universities, and from the schools of law, or from the books which by men eminent in those schools and universities have been published. It is therefore plain that the instruction of the people depends wholly on the right teaching of youth in the universities. But (some may say) are not the universities of England learned enough already to do that? Or is it you who will undertake to teach the universities? Hard questions. Yet to the first, I do not doubt to answer that until towards the latter end of Henry the Eighth, the power of the pope was always upheld against the power of the commonwealth, principally by the universities; and that the doctrines maintained by so many preachers against the sovereign power of the king, and by so many lawyers and others who had their education there, is sufficient argument that, though the universities were not the authors of those false doctrines, they did not know how to plant the true. For in such a contradiction of opinions, it is most certain that they were not sufficiently instructed; and it is no wonder if they still retain a relish of that subtle liquor with which they were first seasoned, against the civil authority. But to the latter question, it is neither fitting nor needful for me to say either yes or no: for any man who sees what I am doing may easily perceive what I think.

The safety of the people further requires of him, or them, who have the sovereign power, that justice be equally administered to all classes of people; that is, that as well the rich and mighty as the poor and obscure may be righted of the injuries done them — so that the great may have no greater hope of impunity, when they do violence, dishonour, or any injury to the meaner sort, than the meaner have when one of them does the like to one of the great. For in this consists equity, to which, being a precept of the law of nature, a sovereign is as much subject as any of the lowest of his people. All breaches of the law are offences against the commonwealth, but some are also against private persons. Those that concern the commonwealth only may, without breach of equity, be pardoned; for every man may pardon what is done against himself, according to his own discretion. But an offence against a private man cannot in equity be pardoned without the consent of the man who is injured, or reasonable satisfaction.

The inequality of subjects proceeds from the acts of sovereign power, and so has no more place in the presence of the sovereign (that is, in a court of justice) than the inequality between kings and their subjects in the presence of the King of Kings. The honour of great persons is to be valued for their beneficence, and for the aids they give to men of inferior rank, or not at all. And the violences, oppressions, and injuries they do are not extenuated, but aggravated, by the greatness of their persons, because they have least need to commit them. The consequences of this partiality toward the great proceed in this way: impunity makes insolence; insolence, hatred; and hatred, an endeavour to pull down all oppressing and contumelious greatness, even at the cost of the ruin of the commonwealth.

To equal justice also belongs the equal imposition of taxes, the equality of which depends not on the equality of riches but on the equality of the debt that every man owes to the commonwealth for his defence. It is not enough for a man to labour for the maintenance of his life; he must also fight (if need be) for the securing of his labour. Men must either do as the Jews did after their return from captivity, in rebuilding the temple — build with one hand and hold the sword in the other — or else they must hire others to fight for them. For the impositions laid on the people by the sovereign power are nothing but the wages due to those who hold the public sword, to defend private men in the exercise of their several trades and callings. Since then the benefit that every man receives from this is the enjoyment of life, which is equally dear to poor and rich, the debt which a poor man owes those who defend his life is the same as the debt a rich man owes for the defence of his — except that the rich, who have the service of the poor, may be debtors not only for their own persons but for many more. From which it follows that the equality of imposition consists rather in the equality of what is consumed than in the equality of the riches of the persons consuming it. For what reason is there that he who labours much, and sparing the fruits of his labour consumes little, should be more charged than he who, living idly, gets little and spends all he gets — since the one has no more protection from the commonwealth than the other? But when the impositions are laid on the things men consume, every man pays equally for what he uses; nor is the commonwealth defrauded by the luxurious waste of private men.

And whereas many men, by unavoidable accident, become unable to maintain themselves by their labour, they ought not to be left to the charity of private persons but to be provided for (so far as the necessities of nature require) by the laws of the commonwealth. For as it is uncharitable in any man to neglect the helpless, so it is in the sovereign of a commonwealth to expose them to the hazard of such uncertain charity.

But for those with strong bodies, the case is otherwise: they are to be forced to work; and to take away the excuse of not finding employment, there ought to be such laws as may encourage all kinds of arts — navigation, agriculture, fishing, and all kinds of manufacture that require labour. The multitude of the poor (and yet strong) people still increasing, they are to be transplanted into countries not sufficiently inhabited; where, nevertheless, they are not to exterminate those they find there, but to constrain them to live closer together, and not to range over a great deal of ground, snatching what they find, but to court each little plot with art and labour, to give them their sustenance in due season. And when all the world is overburdened with inhabitants, then the last remedy of all is war, which provides for every man by victory or death.

To the care of the sovereign belongs the making of good laws. But what is a good law? By a good law I do not mean a just law: for no law can be unjust. The law is made by the sovereign power, and all that is done by such power is warranted and owned by every one of the people; and what every man wills so to be, no man can say is unjust. It is in the laws of a commonwealth as in the rules of gaming: whatever the gamesters all agree on is injustice to none of them. A good law is one that is needful for the good of the people, and at the same time perspicuous.

For the use of laws (which are only rules authorised) is not to bind the people from all voluntary actions, but to direct and keep them in such a course that they do not hurt themselves by their own impetuous desires, rashness, or indiscretion — as hedges are set not to stop travellers, but to keep them in the way. So a law that is not needful, not having the true end of a law, is not good. A law may be conceived to be good when it is for the benefit of the sovereign, though it is not necessary for the people; but it is not so. For the good of the sovereign and the people cannot be separated. It is a weak sovereign that has weak subjects, and a weak people whose sovereign lacks power to rule them at his will. Unnecessary laws are not good laws, but traps for money — which, where the right of sovereign power is acknowledged, are superfluous; and where it is not acknowledged, are insufficient to defend the people.

Perspicuity consists not so much in the words of the law itself as in a declaration of the causes and motives for which it was made. That is what shows us the meaning of the legislator; and the meaning of the legislator known, the law is more easily understood by few than by many words. For all words are subject to ambiguity; and so multiplication of words in the body of the law is multiplication of ambiguity. Besides, it seems to imply (by too much diligence) that whoever can evade the words is beyond the compass of the law — and this is a cause of many unnecessary processes. For when I consider how short the laws of ancient times were, and how they grew by degrees still longer, I seem to see a contest between the framers and the pleaders of the law: the former seeking to fence the latter in, the latter seeking to evade their fences — and the pleaders have got the victory. So it belongs to the office of a legislator (such as in all commonwealths is the supreme representative, whether one man or an assembly) to make the reason perspicuous why the law was made, and to keep the body of the law itself as short, in as proper and significant terms, as may be.

It also belongs to the office of the sovereign to make a right application of punishments and rewards. And since the end of punishing is not revenge and the discharge of anger, but the correction of either the offender or, by his example, of others, the severest punishments are to be inflicted for the crimes that are of most danger to the public — such as those that proceed from malice toward the established government; those that spring from contempt of justice; those that provoke indignation in the multitude; and those that, going unpunished, seem authorised — as when they are committed by sons, servants, or favourites of men in authority. For indignation carries men not only against the doers and authors of injustice, but against any power that is likely to protect them — as in the case of Tarquin, who, for the insolent act of one of his sons, was driven out of Rome, and the monarchy itself dissolved. But for crimes of infirmity, such as those that proceed from great provocation, from great fear, great need, or from ignorance whether the act is a great crime or not, there is often room for leniency without prejudice to the commonwealth — and leniency, where there is room for it, is required by the law of nature. The punishment of the leaders and teachers in a commotion — not of the poor seduced people — when they are punished, can benefit the commonwealth by their example. To be severe to the people is to punish that ignorance which may in great part be imputed to the sovereign, whose fault it was that they were no better instructed.

In the same way, it belongs to the office and duty of the sovereign to apply his rewards always in such a way that benefit to the commonwealth may arise from them — in which consists their use and end; and this is done when those who have well served the commonwealth are, with as little expense of the common treasure as is possible, so well recompensed that others may be encouraged both to serve the same as faithfully as they can, and to study the arts by which they may be enabled to do it better. To buy with money or with preferment, from a popular ambitious subject, his being quiet and desisting from making ill impressions on the people's minds, has nothing of the nature of reward (which is ordained not for disservice but for past service), nor any sign of gratitude, but of fear; nor does it tend to the benefit but to the damage of the public. It is a contest with ambition, like that of Hercules with the monster Hydra, who, having many heads, for every one that was vanquished, three more sprang up. For in the same way, when the stubbornness of one popular man is overcome with reward, many more arise (by the example) who do the same mischief in the hope of like benefit. And as all sorts of manufacture, so also malice increases by being made vendible. And though sometimes a civil war may be deferred by such ways as that, the danger nevertheless grows greater, and the public ruin more assured. It is therefore against the duty of the sovereign, to whom the public safety is committed, to reward those who aspire to greatness by disturbing the peace of their country, and not rather to oppose the beginnings of such men with a little danger, than after a longer time with greater.

Another business of the sovereign is to choose good counsellors — I mean those whose advice he is to take in the government of the commonwealth. For this word counsel, consilium (corrupted from considium), has a wide signification, and includes all assemblies of men who sit together, not only to deliberate what is to be done in the future but also to judge of past acts, and of law for the present. I take it here in the first sense only; and in this sense there is no choice of council, neither in a democracy nor in an aristocracy, because the persons counselling are members of the person counselled. The choice of counsellors therefore belongs to monarchy; in which, the sovereign who does not endeavour to choose those who in every kind are the most able does not discharge his office as he ought. The most able counsellors are those who have least hope of benefit from giving evil counsel, and most knowledge of the things that conduce to the peace and defence of the commonwealth. It is a hard matter to know who expects benefit from public troubles; but the signs that guide to a just suspicion include the soothing of the people in their unreasonable, or irremediable, grievances by men whose estates are not sufficient to discharge their accustomed expenses — and these may easily be observed by any one whom it concerns to know it. But to know who has the most knowledge of public affairs is harder still; and those who know them need them a great deal less. For to know who knows the rules of almost any art is a great degree of the knowledge of that art, because no man can be assured of the truth of another's rules but the one who has first been taught to understand them. But the best signs of knowledge of any art are much conversing in it, and constant good effects of it. Good counsel comes not by lot, nor by inheritance; and so there is no more reason to expect good advice from the rich, or noble, in matters of state, than in delineating the dimensions of a fortress — unless we shall think there is no need of method in the study of politics (as there is in the study of geometry), but only to be onlookers; which is not so. For politics is the harder study of the two. Whereas in these parts of Europe it has been taken for a right of certain persons to have place in the highest council of state by inheritance, this is derived from the conquests of the ancient Germans, in which many absolute lords, joining together to conquer other nations, would not enter into the confederacy without such privileges as might be marks of difference in time to follow between their posterity and the posterity of their subjects — which privileges, being inconsistent with the sovereign power, they may seem to keep by the favour of the sovereign; but contending for them as their right, they must inevitably, by degrees, let them go, and have at last no further honour than naturally adheres to their abilities.

And however able the counsellors in any matter may be, the benefit of their counsel is greater when they give each their advice, and the reasons of it, apart, than when they do it in an assembly by way of orations; and when they have premeditated, than when they speak on the sudden. Both because they have more time to survey the consequences of action, and because they are less subject to being carried away into contradiction through envy, emulation, or other passions arising from the difference of opinion.

The best counsel, in those things that concern not other nations but only the ease and benefit the subjects may enjoy by laws that look only inward, is to be taken from the general information and complaints of the people of each province, who are best acquainted with their own wants; and so, when they demand nothing in derogation of the essential rights of sovereignty, they ought to be diligently taken notice of. For without those essential rights (as I have often said before) the commonwealth cannot at all subsist.

A commander-in-chief of an army, if he is not popular, shall neither be loved nor feared as he ought to be by his army, and consequently cannot perform that office with good success. He must therefore be industrious, valiant, affable, generous, and fortunate, that he may gain an opinion both of sufficiency and of loving his soldiers. This is popularity; and it breeds in the soldiers both the desire and the courage to recommend themselves to his favour, and protects the severity of the general in punishing (when need is) mutinous or negligent soldiers. But this love of soldiers (if security is not given of the commander's fidelity) is a dangerous thing to sovereign power, especially when it is in the hands of an unpopular assembly. So it belongs to the safety of the people both that they be good leaders, and faithful subjects, to whom the sovereign commits his armies.

But when the sovereign himself is popular — that is, revered and loved by his people — there is no danger at all from the popularity of a subject. For soldiers are never so generally unjust as to side with their captain (even when they love him) against their sovereign, when they love not only his person but also his cause. So those who have at any time, by violence, suppressed the power of their lawful sovereign, before they could settle themselves in his place, have always had the trouble of contriving titles, to save the people from the shame of receiving them. To have a known right to sovereign power is so popular a quality that the one who has it, for his own part, needs no more, to turn the hearts of his subjects to him, than that they see him able absolutely to govern his own family — nor, on the part of his enemies, more than a disbanding of their armies. For the greatest and most active part of mankind has never until now been well contented with the present.

Concerning the offices of one sovereign toward another (which are comprehended in that law commonly called the law of nations), I need not say anything in this place; because the law of nations and the law of nature are the same thing. And every sovereign has the same right, in procuring the safety of his people, that any private man can have in procuring the safety of his own body. The same law that dictates to men who have no civil government what they ought to do, and what to avoid, with respect to one another, dictates the same to commonwealths — that is, to the consciences of sovereign princes and sovereign assemblies; there being no court of natural justice but in the conscience only, where not man, but God, reigns. His laws (such of them as oblige all mankind), in respect of God as the author of nature, are natural; and in respect of the same God as king of kings, are laws. But of the kingdom of God, both as king of kings and as king also of a peculiar people, I shall speak in the rest of this discourse.

title: Chapter 31. Of the Kingdom of God by Nature
paragraphs: That the condition of mere nature — that is, of absolute liberty, such as belongs to those who are neither sovereigns nor subjects — is anarchy, and the condition of war; that the precepts by which men are guided to avoid that condition are the laws of nature; that a commonwealth without sovereign power is only a word without substance, and cannot stand; that subjects owe to sovereigns simple obedience in all things in which their obedience is not repugnant to the laws of God — all this I have sufficiently proved in what I have already written. There remains, for the entire knowledge of civil duty, only the knowledge of what those laws of God are. For without that, a man does not know, when he is commanded anything by the civil power, whether it is contrary to the law of God or not; and so, either by too much civil obedience he offends the Divine Majesty, or through fear of offending God he transgresses the commandments of the commonwealth. To avoid both of these rocks, it is necessary to know what the divine laws are. And since the knowledge of all law depends on the knowledge of the sovereign power, I shall in what follows say something of the KINGDOM OF GOD.

'God is king, let the earth rejoice,' says the Psalmist (Psalm 96). And again: 'God is king, though the nations be angry; and he that sits on the cherubim, though the earth be moved' (Psalm 98). Whether men will or not, they must always be subject to the divine power. By denying the existence or providence of God, men may shake off their ease, but not their yoke. But to call this power of God — which extends itself not only to man, but also to beasts, to plants, and to inanimate bodies — by the name of kingdom, is only a metaphorical use of the word. For only he is properly said to reign who governs his subjects by his word, and by the promise of rewards to those who obey, and by threats of punishment to those who do not. So subjects in the kingdom of God are not inanimate bodies, nor irrational creatures, because they understand no precepts as his; nor atheists; nor those who do not believe that God has any care of the actions of mankind — because they acknowledge no word as his, and have no hope of his rewards or fear of his threats. Those, then, who believe that there is a God who governs the world, and who has given precepts and set out rewards and punishments to mankind, are God's subjects; all the rest are to be understood as enemies.

To rule by words requires that such words be plainly made known; for otherwise they are no laws. For it belongs to the nature of laws that there be a sufficient and clear promulgation, such as may take away the excuse of ignorance; and in the laws of men this is of one kind only — namely, proclamation, or promulgation by the voice of man. But God declares his laws in three ways: by the dictates of natural reason; by revelation; and by the voice of some man, to whom by the operation of miracles he procures credit with the rest. From this arises a threefold word of God — rational, sensible, and prophetic — to which corresponds a threefold hearing: right reason, supernatural sense, and faith. As for supernatural sense, which consists in revelation or inspiration, no universal laws have been given in that way, because God does not speak in that manner except to particular persons, and to different men different things.

A twofold kingdom of God, natural and prophetic. From the difference between the other two kinds of God's word — rational, and prophetic — there may be attributed to God a twofold kingdom: natural, and prophetic. Natural, in which he governs as many of mankind as acknowledge his providence, by the natural dictates of right reason. And prophetic, in which, having chosen one peculiar nation (the Jews) for his subjects, he governed them — and them only — not only by natural reason, but by positive laws which he gave them through the mouths of his holy prophets. Of the natural kingdom of God I intend to speak in this chapter.

The right of God's sovereignty is derived from his omnipotence. The right of nature by which God reigns over men, and punishes those who break his laws, is to be derived not from his creating them (as if he required obedience as gratitude for his benefits), but from his irresistible power. I have formerly shown how the sovereign right arises from pact; to show how the same right may arise from nature requires no more than to show in what case it is never taken away. Since all men by nature had right to all things, each had a right to reign over all the rest. But because this right could not be obtained by force, it concerned the safety of every one to lay by that right, and by common consent to set up men, with sovereign authority, to rule and defend them. Whereas if there had been any one man of irresistible power, there would have been no reason why he should not by that power have ruled and defended both himself and them, according to his own discretion. To those, therefore, whose power is irresistible, dominion over all men adheres naturally by their excellence of power; and consequently it is from that power that the kingdom over men, and the right of afflicting men at his pleasure, belongs naturally to God Almighty — not as creator and gracious, but as omnipotent. And though punishment is due for sin only (because by that word is meant affliction for sin), the right of afflicting is not always derived from men's sin, but from God's power.

This question — 'Why do evil men often prosper, and good men suffer adversity?' — has been much disputed by the ancients, and is the same as ours: 'By what right does God dispense the prosperities and adversities of this life?' It is of such difficulty that it has shaken the faith not only of the vulgar but of philosophers, and, what is more, of the saints, concerning divine providence. 'How good,' says David, 'is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart; and yet my feet were almost gone, my treadings had well-nigh slipped; for I was grieved at the wicked, when I saw the ungodly in such prosperity.' And Job — how earnestly does he expostulate with God about the many afflictions he suffered, notwithstanding his righteousness! This question, in the case of Job, is decided by God himself — not by arguments derived from Job's sin but from his own power. For whereas the friends of Job drew their arguments from his affliction to his sin, and he defended himself by the conscience of his innocence, God himself takes up the matter, and having justified the affliction by arguments drawn from his power (such as: 'Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?' and the like), both approved Job's innocence and reproved the erroneous doctrine of his friends. Conformable to this doctrine is the sentence of our Saviour concerning the man born blind, in these words: 'Neither has this man sinned, nor his fathers; but that the works of God might be made manifest in him.' And though it is said that 'death entered into the world by sin' (by which is meant that if Adam had never sinned, he would never have died — that is, would never have suffered any separation of his soul from his body), it does not follow from that that God could not justly have afflicted him, even if he had not sinned, as he afflicts other living creatures that cannot sin.

Having spoken of the right of God's sovereignty, as grounded only on nature, we are next to consider what are the divine laws, or dictates of natural reason — which laws concern either the natural duties of one man to another, or the honour naturally due to our divine sovereign. The first are the same laws of nature of which I have already spoken in the 14th and 15th chapters of this treatise: namely, equity, justice, mercy, humility, and the rest of the moral virtues. It remains, then, that we consider what precepts are dictated to men, by their natural reason alone, without any other word of God, touching the honour and worship of the Divine Majesty.

Honour consists in the inward thought and opinion of the power and goodness of another; and therefore to honour God is to think as highly of his power and goodness as is possible. The external signs of that opinion, appearing in the words and actions of men, are called worship — which is one part of what the Latins understand by the word cultus. For cultus signifies properly and constantly that labour which a man bestows on anything with a purpose to make benefit by it. Now the things from which we make benefit are either subject to us — and the profit they yield follows the labour we bestow on them, as a natural effect — or they are not subject to us, but answer our labour according to their own wills. In the first sense, the labour bestowed on the earth is called culture; and the education of children is a culture of their minds. In the second sense, where men's wills are to be wrought to our purpose, not by force but by complaisance, it signifies as much as courting — that is, the winning of favour by good offices, by praises, by acknowledging their power, and by whatever is pleasing to those from whom we look for any benefit. And this is properly worship; in which sense Publicola is understood as a worshipper of the people, and Cultus Dei as the worship of God.

From internal honour, consisting in the opinion of power and goodness, arise three passions: love, which has reference to goodness; and hope and fear, which relate to power. And three parts of external worship: praise, magnifying, and blessing. The subject of praise is goodness; the subject of magnifying and blessing is power, and the effect of it, felicity. Praise and magnifying are signified both by words and by actions: by words, when we say a man is good or great; by actions, when we thank him for his bounty and obey his power. The opinion of the happiness of another can only be expressed by words.

There are some signs of honour (both in attributes and in actions) that are so by nature — as among attributes: good, just, generous, and the like; and among actions: prayers, thanks, and obedience. Others are so by institution, or custom of men, and in some times and places are honourable, in others dishonourable, in others indifferent — such as the gestures used in salutation, prayer, and thanksgiving, used differently in different times and places. The former is natural worship; the latter, arbitrary.

And of arbitrary worship there are two kinds: it is sometimes commanded, sometimes voluntary. Commanded, when it is such as the one being worshipped requires; free, when it is such as the worshipper thinks fit. When it is commanded, it is not the words or gestures but the obedience that is the worship. But when free, the worship consists in the opinion of the beholders; for if to them the words or actions by which we intend honour seem ridiculous, and tending to contempt, they are not worship; because a sign is not a sign to him who gives it, but to him to whom it is made — that is, to the spectator.

Again, there is a public and a private worship. Public is the worship that a commonwealth performs, as one person. Private is that which a private person offers. Public, in respect of the whole commonwealth, is free; but in respect of particular men it is not so. Private worship is, in secret, free; but in the sight of the multitude it is never without some restraint, either from the laws or from the opinion of men — which is contrary to the nature of liberty.

The end of worship among men is power. For where a man sees another worshipped, he supposes him powerful, and is the readier to obey him — which makes his power greater. But God has no ends; the worship we do him proceeds from our duty, and is directed, according to our capacity, by those rules of honour which reason dictates to be done by the weak to the more powerful, in the hope of benefit, or for fear of damage, or in thankfulness for good already received from them.

That we may know what worship of God is taught us by the light of nature, I will begin with his attributes. Where, first, it is plain that we ought to attribute to him existence; for no man can have the will to honour what he thinks not to have any being.

Second, that those philosophers who said the world, or the soul of the world, was God, spoke unworthily of him, and denied his existence; for by God is meant the cause of the world; and to say the world is God is to say there is no cause of it, that is, no God.
Third, to say the world was not created but eternal (since what is eternal has no cause) is to deny that there is a God.

Fourth, that those who (as they think) attribute ease to God, and so take from him the care of mankind, take from him his honour; for it takes away men's love and fear of him, which is the root of honour.

Fifth, in those things that signify greatness and power, to say he is finite is not to honour him; for it is not a sign of the will to honour God to attribute to him less than we can, and finite is less than we can — because to finite, it is easy to add more.
Nor is it to honour him, to say that we conceive, or imagine, or have an idea of him in our mind; for whatever we conceive is finite.
Nor to attribute to him parts, or totality, which are attributes only of things finite.
Nor to say he is in this place or that; for whatever is in a place is bounded and finite.
Nor that he is moved, or rests; for both of these attributes ascribe to him place.

Nor that there are more gods than one; because it implies them all finite — for there cannot be more than one infinite. Nor to ascribe to him (unless metaphorically, meaning not the passion but the effect) passions that partake of grief — such as repentance, anger, mercy; or of want — such as appetite, hope, desire; or any passive faculty. For passion is power limited by something else.
And so when we ascribe to God a will, it is not to be understood as the will of man, for a rational appetite, but as the power by which he effects every thing.

Likewise when we attribute to him sight, and other acts of sense, as also knowledge and understanding (which in us are nothing but a tumult of the mind raised by external things that press the organic parts of a man's body) — for there is no such thing in God; and being things that depend on natural causes, they cannot be attributed to him.

He who will attribute to God nothing but what is warranted by natural reason must use either such negative attributes as 'infinite,' 'eternal,' 'incomprehensible'; or superlatives, such as 'most high,' 'most great,' and the like; or indefinite terms, such as 'good,' 'just,' 'holy,' 'creator' — and in such a sense as if he meant not to declare what God is (for that would be to circumscribe him within the limits of our fancy), but how much we admire him, and how ready we would be to obey him; which is a sign of humility, and of a will to honour him as much as we can. For there is only one name to signify our conception of his nature, and that is I AM; and only one name of his relation to us, and that is GOD — in which is contained Father, King, and Lord.

Concerning the actions of divine worship, it is a most general precept of reason that they be signs of the intention to honour God; such as are, first, prayers. For not the carvers, when they made images, were thought to make them gods, but the people that prayed to them.

Second, thanksgiving — which differs from prayer in divine worship in nothing else than that prayers precede, and thanks follow, the benefit; the end both of the one and the other being to acknowledge God as the author of all benefits, both past and to come.
Third, gifts; that is, sacrifices and oblations (if they are of the best) are signs of honour, for they are thanksgivings.

Fourth, not to swear by any but God is naturally a sign of honour; for it is a confession that God only knows the heart, and that no man's wit or strength can protect a man against God's vengeance on the perjured.

Fifth, it is a part of rational worship to speak considerately of God, for it shows a fear of him, and fear is a confession of his power. From this it follows that the name of God is not to be used rashly, and to no purpose; for that is as much as 'in vain.' And it is to no purpose unless it is by way of an oath, and by order of the commonwealth, to make judgements certain — or between commonwealths, to avoid war. And to dispute of God's nature is contrary to his honour. For it is supposed that in this natural kingdom of God there is no other way to know any thing but by natural reason — that is, from the principles of natural science. And these are so far from teaching us anything of God's nature that they cannot teach us even our own nature, nor the nature of the smallest creature living. So when men, from the principles of natural reason, dispute of the attributes of God, they only dishonour him: for in the attributes we give to God we are not to consider the signification of philosophical truth, but the signification of pious intention, to do him the greatest honour we are able. From want of this consideration have proceeded the volumes of disputation about the nature of God which tend not to his honour but to the honour of our own wits and learning, and are nothing but inconsiderate and vain abuses of his sacred name.

Sixth, in prayers, thanksgivings, offerings, and sacrifices, it is a dictate of natural reason that they each be, in their kind, the best, and the most significant of honour. For example, that prayers and thanksgivings be made in words and phrases that are not sudden, nor light, nor plebeian, but beautiful and well composed; for otherwise we do not God as much honour as we can. So the heathens did absurdly to worship images as gods; but their doing it in verse, and with music, both of voice and of instruments, was reasonable. Also, that the beasts they offered in sacrifice, and the gifts they offered, and their actions in worshipping, were full of submission and commemorative of benefits received, was in keeping with reason — as proceeding from an intention to honour him.

Seventh, reason directs not only to worship God in secret, but also, and especially, in public, and in the sight of men. For without that, what in honour is most acceptable — the procuring of others to honour him — is lost.

Lastly, obedience to his laws (that is, in this case, to the laws of nature) is the greatest worship of all. For as obedience is more acceptable to God than sacrifice, so also to make light of his commandments is the greatest of all contumelies. And these are the laws of that divine worship which natural reason dictates to private men.

But since a commonwealth is only one person, it ought also to exhibit to God only one worship; which it does when it commands that worship to be offered, by private men, publicly. And this is public worship, whose property is to be uniform: for actions done differently by different men cannot be called a public worship. And so where many sorts of worship are allowed, proceeding from the different religions of private men, it cannot be said that there is any public worship, or that the commonwealth is of any religion at all.

And because words (and consequently the attributes of God) have their meaning by the agreement and constitution of men, those attributes are to be held significative of honour which men intend shall be so. And whatever may be done by the wills of particular men, where there is no law but reason, may be done by the will of the commonwealth, by civil laws. And because a commonwealth has no will, nor makes any laws, but those that are made by the will of him, or them, who have the sovereign power, it follows that those attributes which the sovereign ordains, in the worship of God, as signs of honour, ought to be taken and used as such by private men in their public worship.

But because not all actions are signs by constitution — some are naturally signs of honour, others of contempt — the latter (which are those that men are ashamed to do in the sight of those they revere) cannot by human power be made part of divine worship; nor can the former (such as decent, modest, humble behaviour) ever be separated from it. But whereas there are an infinite number of actions and gestures of an indifferent nature, those of them which the commonwealth shall ordain to be publicly and universally used as signs of honour, and part of God's worship, are to be taken and used as such by the subjects. And the saying in Scripture, 'It is better to obey God than men,' has place in the kingdom of God by pact, not by nature.

Having thus briefly spoken of the natural kingdom of God, and of his natural laws, I will add to this chapter only a short statement on his natural punishments. There is no action of man in this life that is not the beginning of so long a chain of consequences that no human providence is high enough to give a man a prospect of its end. And in this chain are linked together both pleasing and unpleasing events, in such a way that he who will do anything for his pleasure must engage himself to suffer all the pains annexed to it; and these pains are the natural punishments of those actions which are the beginning of more harm than good. Hereby it comes to pass that intemperance is naturally punished with diseases; rashness, with mischances; injustice, with the violence of enemies; pride, with ruin; cowardice, with oppression; the negligent government of princes, with rebellion; and rebellion, with slaughter. For since punishments are consequent on the breach of laws, natural punishments must be naturally consequent on the breach of the laws of nature, and so follow them as their natural, not arbitrary, effects.

And so far concerning the constitution, nature, and right of sovereigns, and concerning the duty of subjects, derived from the principles of natural reason. And now, considering how different this doctrine is from the practice of the greater part of the world — especially of these western parts, which have received their moral learning from Rome and Athens — and how much depth of moral philosophy is required in those who have the administration of the sovereign power, I am at the point of believing this work of mine to be as useless as the commonwealth of Plato. For he too is of the opinion that it is impossible for the disorders of state, and the change of governments by civil war, ever to be taken away until sovereigns are philosophers. But when I consider again that the science of natural justice is the only science necessary for sovereigns and their principal ministers, and that they need not be charged with the mathematical sciences (as by Plato they are) further than to encourage men by good laws to the study of them; and that neither Plato nor any other philosopher up to now has put into order, and sufficiently or probably proved, all the theorems of moral doctrine, by which men may learn how both to govern and to obey, I recover some hope that one time or other this writing of mine may fall into the hands of a sovereign, who will consider it himself (for it is short, and I think clear), without the help of any interested or envious interpreter; and by the exercise of entire sovereignty, in protecting the public teaching of it, will convert this truth of speculation into the utility of practice.

title: Chapter 32. Of the Principles of Christian Politics
paragraphs: I have derived the rights of sovereign power, and the duty of subjects, up to this point, from the principles of nature alone — such as experience has found true, or as consent (concerning the use of words) has made so; that is, from the nature of men, known to us by experience, and from definitions (of words essential to all political reasoning) universally agreed upon. But in what I am next to handle — the nature and rights of a CHRISTIAN COMMONWEALTH — much depends on the supernatural revelations of the will of God; and so the ground of my discourse must be not only the natural word of God but also the prophetic.

Nevertheless, we are not to renounce our senses, and our experience; nor (which is the undoubted word of God) our natural reason. For these are the talents he has put into our hands to trade with until the coming again of our blessed Saviour, and so are not to be folded up in the napkin of an implicit faith, but employed in the purchase of justice, peace, and true religion. For though there are many things in God's word above reason — that is, which can neither be demonstrated nor refuted by natural reason — there is nothing contrary to it; and when it seems so, the fault is either in our unskilful interpretation, or in erroneous reasoning.

So when anything written there is too hard for our examination, we are bidden to captivate our understanding to the words, and not to labour by logic in sifting out a philosophical truth from such mysteries as are not comprehensible, and fall under no rule of natural science. For it is with the mysteries of our religion as with wholesome pills for the sick — which, swallowed whole, have the virtue to cure, but, chewed, are for the most part cast up again without effect.

But by the captivity of our understanding is not meant a submission of the intellectual faculty to the opinion of any other man, but of the will to obedience, where obedience is due. For sense, memory, understanding, reason, and opinion are not in our power to change, but are always and necessarily such as the things we see, hear, and consider suggest to us; and so they are not effects of our will, but our will is an effect of them. We captivate our understanding and reason when we forbear contradiction; when we so speak as (by lawful authority) we are commanded; and when we live accordingly. Which in sum is trust, and faith reposed in the one who speaks, even though the mind is incapable of any notion at all from the words spoken.

When God speaks to a man, it must be either directly, or through the mediation of another man to whom he has previously spoken directly himself. How God speaks to a man directly may be well enough understood by those to whom he has so spoken; but how the same should be understood by another is hard, if not impossible, to know. For if a man claims to me that God has spoken to him supernaturally and directly, and I doubt it, I cannot easily see what argument he can produce to oblige me to believe it. It is true that, if he is my sovereign, he may oblige me to obedience — so that I shall not by act or word declare that I do not believe him; but he may not oblige me to think any otherwise than my reason persuades me. But if one who has no such authority over me makes the same claim, there is nothing that compels either belief or obedience.

For to say that God has spoken to him in the Holy Scripture is not to say God has spoken to him directly, but through the mediation of the prophets, or of the apostles, or of the Church — in such manner as he speaks to all other Christian men. To say he has spoken to him in a dream is no more than to say he dreamed that God spoke to him; which is not strong enough to win belief from anyone who knows that dreams are for the most part natural, and may proceed from former thoughts — and that such dreams may come from self-conceit and foolish arrogance, and from a false opinion of one's own godliness or other virtue, by which he thinks he has merited the favour of extraordinary revelation. To say he has seen a vision, or heard a voice, is to say he has dreamed between sleeping and waking; for in such a way a man often naturally takes his dream for a vision, not having well observed his own slumbering. To say he speaks by supernatural inspiration is to say he finds an ardent desire to speak, or some strong opinion of himself, for which he can allege no natural and sufficient reason. So that, though God Almighty can speak to a man by dreams, visions, voice, and inspiration, he obliges no one to believe he has done so to the man who claims it — who (being a man) may err, and (what is more) may lie.

How then can a man to whom God has never revealed his will directly (saving by the way of natural reason) know when he is to obey, or not to obey, his word delivered by one who says he is a prophet? Of the four hundred prophets of whom the king of Israel asked counsel concerning the war he made against Ramoth-Gilead (1 Kings 22), only Micaiah was a true one. The prophet who was sent to prophesy against the altar set up by Jeroboam (1 Kings 13), though a true prophet — as the two miracles done in his presence show him to be one sent from God — was yet deceived by another, old, prophet, who persuaded him, as from the mouth of God, to eat and drink with him. If one prophet can deceive another, what certainty is there of knowing the will of God by any way other than that of reason? To which I answer out of Holy Scripture: there are two marks by which, taken together (not separately), a true prophet is to be known. One is the doing of miracles; the other is the not teaching of any other religion than that which is already established. Apart, I say, neither of these is sufficient. 'If a prophet rise among you,' says Deuteronomy 13:1–5, 'or a dreamer of dreams, and shall pretend the doing of a miracle, and the miracle come to pass; if he say, Let us follow strange gods, which you have not known, you shall not listen to him, etc. But that prophet, and dreamer of dreams, shall be put to death, because he has spoken to you to revolt from the Lord your God.' In these words two things are to be noted. First, that God will not have miracles alone serve as arguments to approve the prophet's calling, but (as it is in the third verse) as an experiment of the constancy of our adherence to himself. For the works of the Egyptian sorcerers, though not as great as those of Moses, were still great miracles. Second, that however great the miracle may be, if it tends to stir up revolt against the king, or against him who governs by the king's authority, the one who does such a miracle is not to be considered otherwise than as sent to make trial of their allegiance. For the words 'revolt from the Lord your God' are in this place equivalent to 'revolt from your king.' For they had made God their king by pact at the foot of Mount Sinai; who ruled them by Moses alone — for he alone spoke with God, and from time to time declared God's commandments to the people. In the same way, after our Saviour Christ had brought his disciples to acknowledge him for the Messiah (that is, for God's anointed, whom the nation of the Jews daily expected for their king, but rejected when he came), he did not fail to warn them of the danger of miracles: 'There shall arise,' he says, 'false Christs, and false prophets, and shall do great wonders and miracles, even to the seducing (if it were possible) of the very elect' (Matthew 24:24). By this it appears that false prophets may have the power of miracles; and yet we are not to take their doctrine for God's word. St Paul says further to the Galatians that 'if I myself, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you than the one I preached, let him be accursed' (Galatians 1:8). That gospel was that Christ was king; so all preaching against the power of the king received, in consequence of these words, is by St Paul accursed. For his speech is addressed to those who, by his preaching, had already received Jesus for the Christ — that is, for king of the Jews.

And as miracles without the preaching of the doctrine God has established, so the preaching of true doctrine without the doing of miracles, is an insufficient argument of immediate revelation. For if a man who teaches no false doctrine should pretend to be a prophet without showing any miracle, he is not, for that pretence, to be the more regarded, as is evident from Deuteronomy 18:21–22: 'If you say in your heart, How shall we know that the word [of the prophet] is not that which the Lord has spoken? — when a prophet has spoken in the name of the Lord, and what he says does not come to pass, that is the word the Lord has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it out of the pride of his own heart; fear him not.' But here a man may ask again: when the prophet has foretold a thing, how shall we know whether it will come to pass or not? For he may foretell it as something to come about after a long time — longer than a man's lifetime — or indefinitely, that it will come about at some time or other; in which case this mark of a prophet is useless. And so the miracles which oblige us to believe a prophet ought to be confirmed by an immediate, or not long deferred, event. So it is plain that the teaching of the religion God has established, and the showing of a present miracle, joined together, were the only marks by which Scripture would have a true prophet — that is, immediate revelation — to be acknowledged; and that neither of them is by itself enough to oblige any other man to regard what he says.

Seeing then that miracles now cease, we have no sign left whereby to acknowledge the pretended revelations or inspirations of any private man; nor any obligation to give ear to any doctrine, further than as it is conformable to the Holy Scriptures, which since the time of our Saviour supply the want of all other prophecy; and from which, by wise and careful reasoning, all rules and precepts necessary to the knowledge of our duty both to God and to man — without enthusiasm or supernatural inspiration — may easily be deduced. And this Scripture is what I shall draw on for the principles of my discourse, concerning the rights of those who are the supreme governors on earth of Christian commonwealths, and the duty of Christian subjects toward their sovereigns. To that end, I shall speak in the next chapter of the books, writers, scope, and authority of the Bible.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 33. Of the Number, Antiquity, Scope, Authority, and Interpreters of the Books of Holy Scripture
paragraphs: By the books of Holy SCRIPTURE are meant those that ought to be the canon — that is, the rules — of Christian life. And because all the rules of life that men are in conscience bound to observe are laws, the question of Scripture is the question of what is law throughout all Christendom, both natural and civil. For though Scripture does not determine what laws each Christian king shall constitute in his own dominions, it does determine what laws he shall not constitute. Since therefore I have already proved that sovereigns in their own dominions are the sole legislators, only those books are canonical — that is, law — in every nation which are established as such by the sovereign authority. It is true that God is the sovereign of all sovereigns, and so, when he speaks to any subject, he ought to be obeyed, whatever any earthly potentate commands to the contrary. But the question is not of obedience to God, but of when, and what, God has said. To subjects who have no supernatural revelation, this can be known only by that natural reason which guided them, for the obtaining of peace and justice, to obey the authority of their several commonwealths — that is, of their lawful sovereigns. According to this obligation, I can acknowledge no other books of the Old Testament to be Holy Scripture except those that have been commanded to be acknowledged as such by the authority of the Church of England. What books these are is well enough known without setting them all out here; and they are the same as those acknowledged by St Jerome — who holds the rest (namely, the Wisdom of Solomon, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobias, the first and second of Maccabees — though he had seen the first in Hebrew — and the third and fourth of Esdras) for Apocrypha. Of the canonical, Josephus, a learned Jew who wrote in the time of the Emperor Domitian, reckons twenty-two, making the number agree with the Hebrew alphabet. St Jerome does the same, though they reckon them differently. For Josephus numbers five books of Moses, thirteen of prophets who wrote the history of their own times (how that agrees with the prophetic writings contained in the Bible we shall see hereafter), and four of hymns and moral precepts. But St Jerome reckons five books of Moses, eight of prophets, and nine of other holy writings, which he calls Hagiographa. The Septuagint — seventy learned Jewish men sent for by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, to translate the Jewish law from Hebrew into Greek — have left us no other books for Holy Scripture in the Greek tongue than the same ones that are received in the Church of England.
As for the books of the New Testament, they are equally acknowledged as canon by all Christian churches, and by all sects of Christians that admit any books at all as canonical.

Who the original writers of the various books of Holy Scripture were has not been made evident by any sufficient testimony from any other history (which is the only proof of matter of fact), nor can it be by any arguments of natural reason — for reason serves only to convince of the truth, not of fact, but of consequence. The light, therefore, that must guide us in this question must be what is held out to us by the books themselves. And this light, though it does not show us the writer of every book, is yet not useless in giving us knowledge of the time when they were written.

And first, for the Pentateuch, it is not argument enough that they were written by Moses just because they are called the five books of Moses — no more than the titles 'The Book of Joshua,' 'The Book of Judges,' 'The Book of Ruth,' and 'The Books of the Kings' are arguments enough to prove that they were written by Joshua, by the Judges, by Ruth, and by the Kings. In titles of books, the subject is marked as often as the writer. 'The History of Livy' denotes the writer; but 'The History of Scanderbeg' is named from the subject. We read in the last chapter of Deuteronomy (verse 6), concerning the sepulchre of Moses, that 'no man knows of his sepulchre to this day' — that is, to the day on which those words were written. It is therefore plain that those words were written after his burial. For it would be a strange interpretation to say that Moses spoke of his own sepulchre (even by prophecy), saying that it was not to be found to that day on which he was yet living. But it may perhaps be alleged that only the last chapter, not the whole Pentateuch, was written by some other man. Let us therefore consider what we find in the book of Genesis, chapter 12, verse 6: 'And Abraham passed through the land, to the place of Shechem, to the plain of Moreh, and the Canaanite was then in the land.' These must be the words of someone writing when the Canaanite was no longer in the land — and consequently not of Moses, who died before he came into it. Likewise in Numbers 21:14, the writer cites another, more ancient, book entitled The Book of the Wars of the Lord, in which were recorded the acts of Moses at the Red Sea and at the brook Arnon. So it is sufficiently plain that the five books of Moses were written after his time, though how long after is not so plain.

But though Moses did not compile those books entirely, and in the form we have them, he wrote everything he is there said to have written: for example, the volume of the law, which is contained, as it seems, in Deuteronomy 11 and the following chapters to chapter 27 — which was also commanded to be written on stones on their entry into the land of Canaan (Deut. 31:9). And this Moses himself wrote, and delivered to the priests and elders of Israel, to be read every seventh year to all Israel at their assembling for the feast of Tabernacles. And this is the law which God commanded that their kings (once they had established that form of government) should take a copy of from the priests and Levites, to lay in the side of the ark (Deut. 31:26); and the same which, having been lost, was long afterward found again by Hilkiah and sent to King Josiah, who, causing it to be read to the people, renewed the covenant between God and them (2 Kings 22:8 and 23:1–3).

That the book of Joshua was also written long after the time of Joshua may be gathered from many places in the book itself. Joshua had set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan as a monument to their crossing (Josh. 4:9); of which the writer says, 'They are there to this day.' For 'to this day' is a phrase that signifies a time past, beyond the memory of man. In the same way, upon the saying of the Lord that he had rolled off from the people the reproach of Egypt, the writer says, 'The place is called Gilgal to this day' (Josh. 5:9) — which would have been improper to say in the time of Joshua. So too of the name of the Valley of Achor, from the trouble Achan raised in the camp, the writer says it 'remains to this day' (Josh. 7:26) — which must therefore have been long after the time of Joshua. There are many other arguments of this kind, as Josh. 8:29; 13:13; 14:14; 15:63.

The same is plain by like arguments for the book of Judges (1:21, 26; 6:24; 10:4; 15:19; 17:6) and for Ruth (1:1), but especially Judges 18:30, where it is said that Jonathan 'and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan, until the day of the captivity of the land.'

That the books of Samuel were also written after his own time, there are the like arguments: 1 Sam. 5:5; 7:13, 15; 27:6; and 30:25 — where, after David had adjudged an equal share of the spoils to those who guarded the baggage as to those who fought, the writer says, 'He made it a statute and an ordinance to Israel to this day.' Again, when David (displeased that the Lord had slain Uzzah for putting out his hand to steady the ark) called the place Perez-Uzzah, the writer says it is called so 'to this day' (2 Sam. 6:4). The time of the writing of that book must therefore be long after the time of the fact — that is, long after the time of David.

As for the two books of the Kings and the two books of the Chronicles, beyond the passages that mention such monuments as the writer says remained to his own day — such as 1 Kings 9:13; 9:21; 10:12; 12:19; 2 Kings 2:22; 8:22; 10:27; 14:7; 16:6; 17:23; 17:34; 17:41; 1 Chron. 4:41; 5:26 — it is sufficient argument that they were written after the captivity in Babylon that their history is continued to that time. For the facts recorded are always more ancient than such books as mention and quote the register; as these books do in various places, referring the reader to the chronicles of the kings of Judah, to the chronicles of the kings of Israel, to the books of the prophet Samuel or the prophet Nathan, of the prophet Ahijah, to the vision of Iddo, to the books of the prophet Shemaiah and of the prophet Iddo.

The books of Ezra and Nehemiah were certainly written after their return from captivity, because their return, the rebuilding of the walls and houses of Jerusalem, the renewal of the covenant, and the ordination of their polity are all contained in them.
The history of Queen Esther is from the time of the captivity, and so the writer must have been of the same time, or after it.

The book of Job has no mark in it of the time when it was written. And though it sufficiently appears (from Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11) that he was no fictitious person, the book itself does not seem to be a history but a treatise on a question much disputed in ancient times — namely, 'why wicked men have often prospered in this world, and good men have been afflicted.' This is the most likely reading because, from the beginning to the third verse of the third chapter (where Job's complaint begins), the Hebrew is (as St Jerome testifies) in prose; and from there to the sixth verse of the last chapter, in hexameter verses; and the rest of that chapter again in prose. So the dispute is all in verse, and the prose is added only as a preface at the beginning and an epilogue at the end. But verse is not the usual style of men who are themselves in great pain, like Job, or of those who come to comfort them, like his friends — yet in philosophy, especially moral philosophy, it was frequent in ancient times.

The Psalms were written for the most part by David, for the use of the choir. To these are added some songs of Moses and other holy men, and some written after the return from the captivity, such as Psalms 137 and 126; whereby it is plain that the Psalter was compiled and put into the form it now has after the return of the Jews from Babylon.

The Proverbs, being a collection of wise and godly sayings — partly of Solomon, partly of Agur the son of Jakeh, and partly of the mother of King Lemuel — cannot probably be thought to have been collected by Solomon rather than by Agur or the mother of Lemuel; and that, though the sentences are theirs, the collecting or compiling of them into this one book was the work of some other godly man who lived after them all.

The books of Ecclesiastes and the Canticles have nothing that was not Solomon's, except perhaps the titles or inscriptions. For 'The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem,' and 'The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's,' seem to have been made for the sake of distinction at the time when the books of Scripture were gathered into one body of the law, so that not only the doctrine but also the authors might be on record.

Of the prophets, the most ancient are Zephaniah, Jonah, Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, and Micah, who lived in the time of Amaziah and Azariah (otherwise Uzziah), kings of Judah.
