But the book of Jonah is not properly a record of his prophecy (for that is contained in these few words: 'Forty days, and Nineveh shall be destroyed'), but a history or narrative of his perverseness in disputing God's commandments; so there is little probability he should be the author, given that he is the subject. But the book of Amos is his prophecy.
Jeremiah, Obadiah, Nahum, and Habakkuk prophesied in the time of Josiah.
Ezekiel, Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah prophesied in the captivity.

When Joel and Malachi prophesied is not evident from their writings. But considering the inscriptions, or titles, of their books, it is plain enough that the whole Scripture of the Old Testament was set forth in the form we have it after the return of the Jews from their captivity in Babylon, and before the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, who had it translated into Greek by seventy men sent to him out of Judea for that purpose. And if the books of Apocrypha (which the Church recommends to us, though not as canonical, yet as profitable books for our instruction) may on this point be credited, the Scripture was set forth in the form we have by Ezra; as may appear from what he himself says in 2 Esdras 14:21–22 (etc.), where, speaking to God, he says, 'Your law is burnt; therefore no man knows the things you have done, or the works that are to begin. But if I have found grace before you, send down the holy Spirit into me, and I shall write all that has been done in the world since the beginning, which were written in your law, that men may find your path, and that those who shall live in the latter days may live.' And verse 45: 'And it came to pass, when the forty days were fulfilled, that the Highest spoke, saying, "The first that you have written, publish openly, that the worthy and unworthy may read it; but keep the seventy last, that you may deliver them only to such as are wise among the people."' And this much concerning the time of the writing of the books of the Old Testament.

The writers of the New Testament all lived less than an age after Christ's ascension, and had all seen our Saviour, or been his disciples, except St Paul and St Luke; and consequently whatever was written by them is as ancient as the time of the apostles. But the time at which the books of the New Testament were received and acknowledged by the Church as their writing is not altogether so ancient. For as the books of the Old Testament come to us from no higher time than that of Ezra, who by the direction of God's Spirit retrieved them when they were lost, so the books of the New Testament — copies of which were not many, nor could easily be all in any one private man's hand — cannot be derived from a higher time than that at which the governors of the Church collected, approved, and recommended them to us as the writings of those apostles and disciples under whose names they go. The first enumeration of all the books, both of the Old and New Testament, is in the Canons of the Apostles, supposed to have been collected by Clement, the first (after St Peter) bishop of Rome. But because that is only supposed, and by many questioned, the Council of Laodicea is the first we know of that recommended the Bible to the then-Christian churches as the writings of the prophets and apostles; and this council was held in the 364th year after Christ. At which time, though ambition had so far prevailed on the great doctors of the Church that they no longer esteemed emperors (even Christian ones) as the shepherds of the people, but as sheep; and emperors who were not Christian as wolves; and they endeavoured to pass their doctrine, not as counsel and information from preachers, but as laws from absolute governors; and thought such frauds as tended to make the people the more obedient to Christian doctrine to be pious — yet I am persuaded they did not on that account falsify the Scriptures, even though the copies of the books of the New Testament were in the hands only of the ecclesiastics. For if they had had any such intention, they would surely have made them more favourable to their power over Christian princes, and to civil sovereignty, than they are. I see therefore no reason to doubt that the Old and New Testaments, as we have them now, are the true records of what was done and said by the prophets and apostles. And so perhaps are some of those books which are called Apocrypha, if left out of the canon not for any disagreement of doctrine with the rest, but only because they are not found in the Hebrew. For after the conquest of Asia by Alexander the Great, there were few learned Jews who were not perfect in the Greek tongue. The seventy interpreters who turned the Bible into Greek were all of them Hebrews; and we have extant the works of Philo and Josephus, both Jews, written by them eloquently in Greek. But it is not the writer, but the authority of the Church, that makes a book canonical.

And although these books were written by various men, it is plain that the writers were all endowed with one and the same Spirit, in that they conspire to one and the same end — the setting forth of the rights of the kingdom of God: the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. For the book of Genesis derives the genealogy of God's people from the creation of the world to the going down into Egypt; the other four books of Moses contain the election of God for their king, and the laws he prescribed for their government; the books of Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and Samuel, to the time of Saul, describe the acts of God's people until the time when they cast off God's yoke and called for a king after the manner of their neighbouring nations. The rest of the history of the Old Testament traces the succession of the line of David to the captivity, from which line was to spring the restorer of the kingdom of God — our blessed Saviour, God the Son — whose coming was foretold in the books of the prophets, after whom the evangelists wrote his life, and his actions, and his claim to the kingdom, while he lived on earth. And lastly, the Acts and Epistles of the apostles declare the coming of God the Holy Ghost, and the authority he left with the apostles and their successors for the direction of the Jews and the inviting of the Gentiles. In short, the histories and prophecies of the Old Testament, and the Gospels and Epistles of the New, have all had one and the same scope — to convert men to the obedience of God: first in Moses and the priests; second in the man Christ; and third in the apostles and the successors to apostolic power. For these three at various times represented the person of God: Moses, and his successors the high priests and kings of Judah, in the Old Testament; Christ himself in the time he lived on earth; and the apostles, and their successors, from the day of Pentecost (when the Holy Ghost descended on them) to this day.
The question of the authority of the Scriptures stated.

It is a question much disputed between the various sects of the Christian religion: from where do the Scriptures derive their authority? — which question is also sometimes propounded in other terms, as 'How do we know them to be the word of God?' or 'Why do we believe them to be so?' The difficulty of resolving it arises chiefly from the impropriety of the words in which the question itself is framed. For it is believed on all hands that the first and original author of them is God; so the question disputed is not that. Again, it is plain that none can know they are God's word (though all true Christians believe it) but those to whom God himself has revealed it supernaturally; and so the question is not rightly put as one of our knowledge of it. Lastly, when the question is put in terms of our belief — since some are moved to believe for one reason, and others for another — there can be no one general answer for them all. The question, truly stated, is: by what authority are they made law?

So far as they do not differ from the laws of nature, there is no doubt that they are the law of God, and carry their authority with them, legible to all men who have the use of natural reason; but this is no other authority than that of all other moral doctrine consonant with reason, whose dictates are laws not made, but eternal.

If they are made law by God himself, they are of the nature of written law, which are laws only to those to whom God has so sufficiently published them that no man can excuse himself by saying that he did not know they were his.

He, therefore, to whom God has not supernaturally revealed that they are his — nor that those who published them were sent by him — is not obliged to obey them, by any authority other than his whose commands already have the force of laws; that is, by any other authority than that of the commonwealth, residing in the sovereign, who alone has the legislative power. Again, if it is not the legislative authority of the commonwealth that gives them the force of laws, it must be some other authority derived from God, either private or public. If private, it obliges only the man to whom in particular God has been pleased to reveal it. For if every man were obliged to take for God's law whatever particular men, on the pretext of private inspiration or revelation, should thrust upon him (given how many men, out of pride and ignorance, take their own dreams, extravagant fancies, and madness for testimonies of God's Spirit; or out of ambition, claim such divine testimonies falsely, against their own consciences), it would be impossible that any divine law should be acknowledged. If public, it is the authority of the commonwealth or of the Church. But the Church, if it is one person, is the same thing as a commonwealth of Christians — called a commonwealth, because it consists of men united in one person, their sovereign; and a Church, because it consists of Christian men united in one Christian sovereign. But if the Church is not one person, then it has no authority at all; it can neither command nor do any action; nor is it capable of having any power or right to anything; nor has it any will, reason, or voice — for all these qualities are personal. Now if the whole number of Christians is not contained in one commonwealth, they are not one person; nor is there a universal Church that has any authority over them; and therefore the Scriptures are not made laws by the universal Church. Or, if it is one commonwealth, then all Christian monarchs and states are private persons, and subject to being judged, deposed, and punished by a universal sovereign of all Christendom. So the question of the authority of the Scriptures is reduced to this: 'Whether Christian kings, and the sovereign assemblies in Christian commonwealths, are absolute in their own territories, immediately under God; or subject to one vicar of Christ, set over the universal Church, to be judged, condemned, deposed, and put to death, as he shall think expedient or necessary for the common good.'

This question cannot be resolved without a more particular consideration of the kingdom of God; from which also we are to judge of the authority of interpreting the Scripture. For whoever has lawful power over any writing to make it law has the power also to approve, or disapprove, the interpretation of the same.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 34. Of the Signification of Spirit, Angel, and Inspiration in the Books of Holy Scripture
paragraphs: Since the foundation of all true reasoning is the constant meaning of words — which in the doctrine that follows depends not (as in natural science) on the will of the writer, nor (as in common conversation) on common usage, but on the sense the words carry in Scripture — it is necessary, before I proceed any further, to determine, out of the Bible, the meaning of those words which by their ambiguity may render what I am to infer from them obscure or open to dispute. I will begin with the words BODY and SPIRIT, which in the language of the Schools are called substances corporeal and incorporeal.

The word body, in its most general acceptation, signifies what fills or occupies some certain space, or imagined place; and depends not on the imagination, but is a real part of what we call the universe. For the universe being the aggregate of all bodies, no real part of it is not also body, nor is anything properly a body that is not also part of (that aggregate of all bodies) the universe. The same word, because bodies are subject to change — that is, to variety of appearance to the senses of living creatures — is also called substance; that is to say, subject to various accidents: sometimes to be moved, sometimes to stand still; to seem to our senses sometimes hot, sometimes cold; sometimes of one colour, smell, taste, or sound, sometimes of another. And this diversity of seeming (produced by the diversity of bodies acting on the organs of our sense) we attribute to alterations of the bodies that operate, and call them accidents of those bodies. According to this acceptation of the word, substance and body signify the same thing; and so 'incorporeal substance' are words which, when joined together, destroy one another, as if a man should say 'an incorporeal body.'

But in the sense of common people, not all the universe is called body, but only such parts of it as they can discern by the sense of feeling to resist their force, or by the sense of their eyes to obstruct a further view. So in the common language of men, air, and aerial substances, are not usually taken for bodies, but (as often as men are aware of their effects) are called wind, or breath, or (because some of them are called in Latin spiritus) spirits — as when they call that aerial substance which in the body of any living creature gives it life and motion, vital and animal spirits. But as for those idols of the brain which represent bodies to us where they are not — as in a looking-glass, in a dream, or to a distempered brain awake — these are (as the apostle says generally of all idols) nothing. Nothing at all, I say, there where they seem to be; and in the brain itself, nothing but tumult, proceeding either from the action of the objects, or from the disorderly agitation of the organs of our sense. And men, who are otherwise occupied than to search into their causes, do not know of themselves what to call them; and so may easily be persuaded by those whose knowledge they much revere — some to call them bodies, and to think them made of air compacted by a power supernatural, because the sight judges them corporeal; and some to call them spirits, because the sense of touch discerns nothing, in the place where they appear, to resist their fingers. So the proper meaning of 'spirit' in common speech is either a subtle, fluid, invisible body, or a ghost, or some other idol or phantom of the imagination. As for metaphorical meanings, there are many. For sometimes it is taken for the disposition or inclination of the mind: as when, for a disposition to contradict the sayings of other men, we say a 'spirit of contradiction'; for a disposition to uncleanness, an 'unclean spirit'; for perverseness, a 'froward spirit'; for sullenness, a 'dumb spirit'; and for an inclination to godliness and the service of God, 'the spirit of God.' Sometimes for any eminent ability, or extraordinary passion, or disease of the mind, as when great wisdom is called the 'spirit of wisdom,' and madmen are said to be 'possessed with a spirit.'

Of other meanings of 'spirit' I find none anywhere; and where none of these can satisfy the sense of the word in Scripture, the passage falls outside human understanding, and our faith in it consists not in our opinion but in our submission. As in all places where God is said to be a spirit, or where by 'the spirit of God' is meant God himself. For the nature of God is incomprehensible — that is, we understand nothing of what he is, but only that he is; and so the attributes we give him are not to tell one another what he is, nor to signify our opinion of his nature, but our desire to honour him with such names as we conceive most honourable among ourselves.

Gen. 1:2: 'The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.' Here, if by the Spirit of God is meant God himself, then motion is attributed to God, and consequently place — which are intelligible only of bodies, and not of incorporeal substances. So the passage is above our understanding, which can conceive nothing as moved that does not change place, or that has no dimension; and whatever has dimension is body. But the meaning of those words is best understood by the similar passage in Gen. 8:1: where, when the earth was covered with waters as at the beginning, God, intending to abate them and again to uncover the dry land, uses like words: 'I will bring my spirit upon the earth, and the waters shall be diminished' — in which place by 'spirit' is meant a wind (that is, air, or spirit, moved), which might be called (as in the former passage) the Spirit of God, because it was God's work.
Second, for extraordinary gifts of the understanding.

Gen. 41:38: Pharaoh calls the wisdom of Joseph 'the spirit of God.' For Joseph, having advised him to look out for a wise and discreet man and to set him over the land of Egypt, Pharaoh says: 'Can we find such a man as this is, in whom is the Spirit of God?' And Exod. 28:3: 'You shall speak (says God) to all that are wise hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, to make Aaron garments, to consecrate him.' Where extraordinary understanding — even in making garments — being the gift of God, is called the Spirit of God. The same is found again in Exod. 31:3–6 and 35:31. And in Isaiah 11:2–3, where the prophet, speaking of the Messiah, says: 'The Spirit of the Lord shall abide upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord' — where plainly are meant, not so many ghosts, but so many eminent graces that God would give him.

In the book of Judges, an extraordinary zeal and courage in the defence of God's people is called the Spirit of God; as when it stirred up Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson to deliver them from servitude (Judg. 3:10; 6:34; 11:29; 13:25; 14:6, 19). And of Saul, on the news of the insolence of the Ammonites toward the men of Jabesh-Gilead, it is said (1 Sam. 11:6) that 'the Spirit of God came upon Saul, and his anger (or, as it is in the Latin, his fury) was kindled greatly.' Where it is not probable that a ghost was meant, but an extraordinary zeal to punish the cruelty of the Ammonites. In the same way, by the Spirit of God that came upon Saul when he was among the prophets that praised God in songs and music (1 Sam. 19:20), is to be understood not a ghost, but an unexpected and sudden zeal to join with them in their devotions.
Fourth, for the gift of prediction by dreams and visions.

The false prophet Zedekiah says to Micaiah (1 Kings 22:24): 'Which way went the Spirit of the Lord from me to speak to you?' Which cannot be understood of a ghost; for Micaiah declared, before the kings of Israel and Judah, the outcome of the battle as from a vision, and not as from a spirit speaking in him.

In the same way it appears, in the books of the prophets, that though they spoke 'by the Spirit of God' — that is, by a special grace of prediction — their knowledge of the future was not by a ghost within them, but by some supernatural dream or vision.

Gen. 2:7: it is said, 'God made man of the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils (spiraculum vitae) the breath of life, and man was made a living soul.' There the 'breath of life' inspired by God signifies no more than that God gave him life. And (Job 27:3), 'as long as the spirit of God is in my nostrils' is no more than to say 'as long as I live.' So in Ezek. 1:20, 'the spirit of life was in the wheels' is equivalent to 'the wheels were alive.' And (Ezek. 2:2), 'the spirit entered into me, and set me on my feet' — that is, 'I recovered my vital strength' — not that any ghost, or incorporeal substance, entered into and possessed his body.

In the 11th chapter of Numbers, verse 17: 'I will take (says God) of the spirit which is upon you, and will put it upon them, and they shall bear the burden of the people with you' — that is, upon the seventy elders. Whereupon two of the seventy are said to prophesy in the camp; of whom some complained, and Joshua asked Moses to forbid them, which Moses would not do. Whereby it appears that Joshua did not know they had received authority so to do, and prophesied according to the mind of Moses — that is, by a spirit, or authority, subordinate to his own.

In the like sense we read (Deut. 34:9) that 'Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom,' because Moses had laid his hands on him; that is, because he was ordained by Moses to carry on the work Moses had begun (namely, the bringing of God's people into the promised land), but, prevented by death, could not finish.

In the like sense it is said (Rom. 8:9): 'If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his' — not meaning thereby the ghost of Christ, but a submission to his doctrine. As also (1 John 4:2), 'Hereby you shall know the Spirit of God; every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is of God' — by which is meant the spirit of unfeigned Christianity, or submission to that main article of the Christian faith, that Jesus is the Christ; which cannot be interpreted of a ghost.

Likewise these words (Luke 4:1), 'And Jesus, full of the Holy Ghost' (that is, as expressed in Matt. 4:1 and Mark 1:12, 'of the Holy Spirit'), may be understood as zeal to do the work for which he was sent by God the Father; but to interpret it of a ghost is to say that God himself (for so our Saviour was) was filled with God — which is very improper and insignificant. How we came to translate Spirits by the word Ghosts, which signifies nothing, either in heaven or on earth, but the imaginary inhabitants of man's brain, I do not examine; but this I say: the word 'spirit' in the text signifies no such thing, but either, properly, a real substance, or, metaphorically, some extraordinary ability or affection of the mind, or of the body.

The disciples of Christ, seeing him walking on the sea (Matt. 14:26 and Mark 6:49), supposed him to be a spirit, meaning thereby an aerial body, and not a phantasm. For it is said they all saw him; which cannot be understood of the delusions of the brain (which are not common to many at once, as visible bodies are, but singular, because of the differences in fancies), but only of bodies. In the same way, where he was taken for a spirit by the same apostles (Luke 24:37). So also (Acts 12:15) when St Peter was delivered out of prison, it would not be believed; but when the maid said he was at the door, they said it was his angel — by which must be meant a corporeal substance, or else we must say that the disciples themselves followed the common opinion of both Jews and Gentiles, that some such apparitions were not imaginary but real, and such as needed not the fancy of man for their existence. These the Jews called spirits and angels, good or bad; as the Greeks called the same by the name of daemons. And some such apparitions may be real, and substantial — that is, subtle bodies, which God can form by the same power by which he formed all things, and make use of as ministers and messengers (that is, angels) to declare his will, and to execute the same when he pleases, in extraordinary and supernatural ways. But when he has so formed them, they are substances endowed with dimensions, and take up room, and can be moved from place to place, which is peculiar to bodies; and so they are not incorporeal ghosts, that is, ghosts that are in no place, that is, that are nowhere, that is, that seeming to be something, are nothing. But if 'corporeal' be taken in the most common manner, for those substances perceptible by our external senses, then 'incorporeal substance' is a thing not imaginary but real — namely, a thin substance, invisible, but having the same dimensions that are in grosser bodies.

By the name ANGEL is generally signified a messenger, and most often a messenger of God. And by a messenger of God is signified anything that makes known his extraordinary presence — that is, the extraordinary manifestation of his power, especially by a dream, or vision.

Concerning the creation of angels, nothing is delivered in the Scriptures. That they are spirits is often repeated; but by the name of 'spirit' is signified, both in Scripture and in common usage among Jews and Gentiles, sometimes thin bodies — as the air, the wind, the vital and animal spirits of living creatures — and sometimes the images that rise in the fancy in dreams and visions, which are not real substances but accidents of the brain. Yet when God raises them supernaturally to signify his will, they are not improperly called God's messengers — that is, his angels.

And as the Gentiles commonly conceived the imagery of the brain to be things really subsisting outside them, and not dependent on the fancy, and out of these framed their opinions of daemons, good and evil — which, because they seemed really to subsist, they called substances, and because they could not feel them with their hands, incorporeal — so also the Jews, on the same ground, without anything in the Old Testament that constrained them to it, had generally an opinion (except the sect of the Sadducees) that those apparitions (which God sometimes pleased to produce in the fancy of men for his own service, and so called his angels) were substances, not dependent on the fancy but permanent creatures of God. Those they thought were good to them, they esteemed the angels of God; those they thought would hurt them, they called evil angels, or evil spirits — such as was the spirit of Python, and the spirits of madmen, lunatics, and epileptics. For they esteemed those troubled with such diseases to be daemoniacs.

But if we consider the places of the Old Testament where angels are mentioned, we shall find that in most of them nothing else can be meant by the word 'angel' but some image raised (supernaturally) in the fancy, to signify the presence of God in the execution of some supernatural work; and so in the rest, where their nature is not expressed, it may be understood in the same way.

For we read in Genesis 16 that the same apparition is called not only an angel but God. Where what (verse 7) is called 'the angel of the Lord,' in verse 10 says to Hagar, 'I will multiply your seed exceedingly' — that is, speaks in the person of God. Nor was this apparition a fancy with a shape, but a voice. By which it is plain that 'angel' there signifies nothing but God himself, who caused Hagar supernaturally to apprehend a voice supernatural, testifying God's special presence there. Why therefore may not the angels that appeared to Lot, and are called in Gen. 19:13 men, and to whom — though they were but two — Lot speaks (verse 18) as to one, and that one as God (for the words are, 'And Lot said to them, Oh not so, my Lord') be understood of images of men supernaturally formed in the fancy, as before by 'angel' was understood a fancied voice? When the angel called to Abraham out of heaven, to stay his hand (Gen. 22:11) from slaying Isaac, there was no apparition, but a voice; which nevertheless was called properly enough a messenger, or angel, of God — because it declared God's will supernaturally, and saves the labour of supposing any permanent ghosts. The angels that Jacob saw on the ladder of heaven (Gen. 28:12) were a vision of his sleep — therefore only fancy, and a dream — yet, being supernatural and signs of God's special presence, those apparitions are not improperly called angels. The same is to be understood in Gen. 31:11, where Jacob says: 'The angel of the Lord appeared to me in my sleep.' For an apparition made to a man in his sleep is what all men call a dream, whether such a dream is natural or supernatural; and what there Jacob calls an angel was God himself — for the same angel says (verse 13), 'I am the God of Bethel.'

Also (Exod. 14:9) the angel that went before the army of Israel to the Red Sea, and then came behind it, is (verse 19) the Lord himself; and he appeared not in the form of a beautiful man, but in form (by day) of a pillar of cloud, and (by night) in the form of a pillar of fire. And yet this pillar was the whole apparition, and angel promised to Moses (Exod. 14:9) as the army's guide. For this cloudy pillar is said to have descended and stood at the door of the tabernacle, and to have talked with Moses.

There you see motion and speech, which are commonly attributed to angels, attributed to a cloud — because the cloud served as a sign of God's presence, and was no less an angel than if it had had the form of a man, or of a child of ever so great beauty, or wings, as they are usually painted, for the false instruction of common people. For it is not the shape, but their use, that makes them angels. And their use is to be signs of God's presence in supernatural operations: as when Moses (Exod. 33:14) asked God to go along with the camp (as he had always done before the making of the golden calf), God did not answer 'I will go,' nor 'I will send an angel in my stead,' but: 'My presence shall go with you.'

To mention all the places of the Old Testament where the name of angel is found would be too long. So to take them all at once, I say: there is no text in that part of the Old Testament which the Church of England holds canonical from which we can conclude there is, or has been created, any permanent thing (understood by the name of spirit or angel) that has no quantity, and that may not be, by the understanding, divided — that is, considered in parts, so that one part may be in one place, and the next part in the place next to it; and, in sum, which is not (taking 'body' for what is somewhat, or somewhere) corporeal. But in every place, the sense will bear the interpretation of angel as messenger; as John the Baptist is called an angel, and Christ the angel of the covenant; and as (by the same analogy) the dove and the fiery tongues, in that they were signs of God's special presence, might also be called angels. Though we find in Daniel two names of angels — Gabriel and Michael — it is clear from the text itself (Dan. 12:1) that by Michael is meant Christ, not as an angel but as a prince; and that Gabriel (as with the like apparitions made to other holy men in their sleep) was nothing but a supernatural phantasm, by which it seemed to Daniel, in his dream, that two saints being in conversation, one of them said to the other, 'Gabriel, let us make this man understand his vision.' For God has no need to distinguish his celestial servants by names, which are useful only to the short memories of mortals. Nor in the New Testament is there any passage from which it can be proved that angels (except where they are used for such men as God has made the messengers and ministers of his word or works) are things permanent, and also incorporeal. That they are permanent may be gathered from the words of our Saviour himself (Matt. 25:41), where he says that it shall be said to the wicked on the last day, 'Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels' — which passage is plain for the permanence of evil angels (unless we might think the name 'devil and his angels' refers to the Church's adversaries and their ministers); but then it is repugnant to their immateriality, because everlasting fire is no punishment to impassible substances, such as are all incorporeal things. Angels are therefore not from this proved to be incorporeal. In the same way, where St Paul says (1 Cor. 6:3), 'Know you not that we shall judge the angels?'; and (2 Pet. 2:4), 'For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down into hell'; and (Jude 6), 'And the angels that kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he has reserved in everlasting chains under darkness to the judgement of the last day' — though they prove the permanence of the angelic nature, they confirm also their materiality. And (Matt. 22:30): 'In the resurrection men neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven' — but in the resurrection men shall be permanent, and not incorporeal; so therefore also are the angels.

There are various other places from which the like conclusion may be drawn. To men who understand the meaning of these words 'substance' and 'incorporeal,' when 'incorporeal' is taken not for subtle body, but for not body, they imply a contradiction: so much so that to say that an angel, or a spirit, is (in that sense) an incorporeal substance, is to say in effect that there is no angel nor spirit at all. Considering, therefore, the meaning of the word 'angel' in the Old Testament, and the nature of dreams and visions that happen to men in the ordinary way of nature, I was inclined to this opinion: that angels were nothing but supernatural apparitions of the fancy, raised by the special and extraordinary operation of God, thereby to make his presence and commandments known to mankind, and chiefly to his own people. But the many passages of the New Testament, and our Saviour's own words, and in texts wherein there is no suspicion of corruption of the Scripture, have extorted from my feeble reason an acknowledgement, and a belief, that there are also angels substantial and permanent. But to believe they are in no place — that is, nowhere, that is, nothing — as those (though indirectly) say who will have them incorporeal, cannot by Scripture be made out.

On the meaning of the word 'spirit' depends that of the word INSPIRATION; which must either be taken properly — and then it is nothing but the blowing into a man of some thin and subtle air, or wind, in such a manner as a man fills a bladder with his breath — or, if spirits are not corporeal but have their existence only in the fancy, it is nothing but the blowing in of a phantasm; which is improper to say, and impossible — for phantasms are not, but only seem to be, something. That word, therefore, is used in Scripture metaphorically only. As in Gen. 2:7, where it is said that God inspired into man the breath of life, no more is meant than that God gave him vital motion. For we are not to think that God made first a living breath, and then blew it into Adam after he was made, whether that breath were real or seeming; but only as it is said (Acts 17:25), 'that he gave him life and breath' — that is, made him a living creature. And where it is said (2 Tim. 3:16), 'All Scripture is given by inspiration from God,' speaking there of the Scripture of the Old Testament, it is an easy metaphor, to signify that God inclined the spirit, or mind, of those writers to write what should be useful in teaching, reproving, correcting, and instructing men in the way of righteous living. But where St Peter (2 Pet. 1:21) says that 'prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but the holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit,' by the Holy Spirit is meant the voice of God in a dream, or supernatural vision, which is not inspiration. Nor when our Saviour, breathing on his disciples, said 'Receive the Holy Spirit,' was that breath the Spirit, but a sign of the spiritual graces he gave them. And though it is said of many — and of our Saviour himself — that he was full of the Holy Spirit, that fullness is not to be understood as the infusion of the substance of God, but as an accumulation of his gifts, such as the gift of sanctity of life, of tongues, and the like, whether attained supernaturally or by study and industry — for in all cases they are the gifts of God. So likewise where God says (Joel 2:28), 'I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions,' we are not to understand it in the proper sense, as if his Spirit were like water, subject to effusion or infusion; but as if God had promised to give them prophetic dreams and visions. For the proper use of the word 'infused,' in speaking of the graces of God, is an abuse of it; for those graces are virtues, not bodies, to be carried here and there and to be poured into men as into barrels.

In the same way, to take inspiration in the proper sense, or to say that good spirits entered into men to make them prophesy, or evil spirits into those who became frenetic, lunatic, or epileptic, is not to take the word in the sense of Scripture. For 'spirit' there is taken for the power of God, working by causes unknown to us. As also (Acts 2:2) the wind that is there said to fill the house in which the apostles were assembled on the day of Pentecost is not to be understood as the Holy Spirit, which is the deity itself, but as an external sign of God's special working on their hearts, to effect in them the internal graces and holy virtues he thought necessary for the performance of their apostleship.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 35. Of the Signification in Scripture of Kingdom of God, of Holy, Sacred, and Sacrament
paragraphs: The Kingdom of God in the writings of divines, and especially in sermons and treatises of devotion, is taken most commonly for eternal felicity after this life, in the highest heaven, which they also call the kingdom of glory; and sometimes for (the earnest of that felicity) sanctification, which they call the kingdom of grace. But it is never taken for monarchy — that is, for the sovereign power of God over subjects acquired by their own consent — which is the proper meaning of 'kingdom.'

On the contrary, I find that the KINGDOM OF GOD signifies, in most places of Scripture, a kingdom properly so called, constituted by the votes of the people of Israel in a peculiar way: in which they chose God for their king by a covenant made with him, on God's promising them the possession of the land of Canaan. And only seldom does it have a metaphorical sense, and then it is taken for dominion over sin (and only in the New Testament), because such a dominion as that, every subject shall have in the kingdom of God, and without prejudice to the sovereign.

From the very creation, God not only reigned over all men naturally by his might; he also had peculiar subjects, whom he commanded by a voice, as one man speaks to another. In that way he reigned over Adam, and gave him a commandment to abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; which when Adam disobeyed but tasted of it, taking upon himself to be as God, judging between good and evil not by his Creator's commandment but by his own sense, his punishment was the deprivation of the state of eternal life in which God had at first created him. And afterwards God punished his posterity, for their vices, all but eight persons, with a universal deluge; and in these eight consisted the kingdom of God at that time.

After this, it pleased God to speak to Abraham, and (Gen. 17:7–8) to make a covenant with him in these words: 'I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you in their generations, for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. And I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land in which you are a stranger, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession.' And as a memorial and a token of this covenant, he ordains (verse 11) the sacrament of circumcision. This is what is called the Old Covenant, or Testament, and contains a contract between God and Abraham, by which Abraham obliges himself, and his posterity, in a peculiar way, to be subject to God's positive law — for to the moral law he was obliged already, as by an oath of allegiance. And though the name 'king' is not yet given to God, nor 'kingdom' to Abraham and his seed, the thing is the same: namely, an institution by pact of God's peculiar sovereignty over the seed of Abraham. This in the renewing of the same covenant by Moses at Mount Sinai is expressly called a peculiar kingdom of God over the Jews; and it is of Abraham (not of Moses) that St Paul says (Rom. 4:11) he is the 'father of the faithful' — that is, of those who are loyal, and do not violate their allegiance sworn to God, then by circumcision, and afterwards in the new covenant by baptism.
That the kingdom of God is properly his civil sovereignty over a peculiar people by pact.

This covenant, at the foot of Mount Sinai, was renewed by Moses (Exod. 19:5), where the Lord commands Moses to speak to the people in this way: 'If you will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then you shall be a peculiar people to me, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a sacerdotal kingdom, and a holy nation.' For 'peculiar people,' the Vulgate Latin has peculium de cunctis populis; the English translation made at the beginning of the reign of King James has 'a peculiar treasure unto me above all nations'; and the Geneva French, 'the most precious jewel of all nations.' But the truest translation is the first, because it is confirmed by St Paul himself (Tit. 2:14), where he says, alluding to that place, that our blessed Saviour 'gave himself for us, that he might purify to himself a peculiar (that is, an extraordinary) people.' For the word in the Greek is periousios, which is commonly opposed to the word epiousios; and as epiousios signifies 'ordinary,' 'daily,' or (as in the Lord's Prayer) 'of daily use,' so the other signifies that which is overplus, and stored up, and enjoyed in a special manner — which the Latins call peculium. And this meaning of the passage is confirmed by the reason God gives for it, which follows immediately, when he adds 'For all the earth is mine' — as if he should say: 'All the nations of the world are mine; but it is not so that you are mine, but in a special manner.' For they are all his by reason of his power; but you shall be mine by your own consent and covenant — which is an addition to his ordinary title to all nations.

The same is again confirmed in express words in the same text: 'You shall be to me a sacerdotal kingdom, and a holy nation.' The Vulgate has Regnum Sacerdotale, which agrees with the translation of that passage (1 Pet. 2:9) Sacerdotium Regale, a 'royal priesthood'; as also with the institution itself, by which no man might enter into the Sanctum Sanctorum — that is, no man might inquire of God's will immediately from God himself — except the high priest only. The English translation already mentioned, following that of Geneva, has 'a kingdom of priests,' which is either meant of the succession of one high priest after another, or else it does not accord with St Peter, nor with the exercise of the high priesthood. For there was never any but the high priest only who was to inform the people of God's will; nor was any convocation of priests ever allowed to enter into the Sanctum Sanctorum.

Again, the title of a 'holy nation' confirms the same. For 'holy' signifies that which is God's by special, not by general, right. All the earth (as is said in the text) is God's; but all the earth is not called holy — only that which is set apart for his special service, as the nation of the Jews was. It is therefore plain enough by this one passage that by the kingdom of God is properly meant a commonwealth, instituted (by the consent of those who were to be subject to it) for their civil government, and for the regulating of their behaviour not only toward God their king, but also toward one another in point of justice, and toward other nations both in peace and in war; which was properly a kingdom, in which God was king and the high priest was to be (after the death of Moses) his sole viceroy, or lieutenant.

But there are many other places that clearly prove the same. First (1 Sam. 8:7), when the elders of Israel (grieved by the corruption of the sons of Samuel) demanded a king, Samuel was displeased with this, and prayed to the Lord; and the Lord, answering, said to him: 'Listen to the voice of the people, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.' From which it is evident that God himself was then their king; and that Samuel did not command the people, but only delivered to them what God from time to time appointed him.

Again, (1 Sam. 12:12), where Samuel says to the people: 'When you saw that Nahash, king of the children of Ammon, came against you, you said to me, Nay, but a king shall reign over us — when the Lord your God was your king.' It is plain that God was their king, and governed the civil state of their commonwealth.

And after the Israelites had rejected God, the prophets foretold his restoration. As in Isaiah 24:23: 'Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem' — where he speaks expressly of his reign in Zion and Jerusalem; that is, on earth. And (Micah 4:7), 'And the Lord shall reign over them in Mount Zion'; this Mount Zion is in Jerusalem, on the earth. And (Ezek. 20:33), 'As I live, says the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand, and a stretched out arm, and with fury poured out, I will rule over you'; and (verse 37) 'I will cause you to pass under the rod, and I will bring you into the bond of the covenant' — that is, 'I will reign over you, and make you stand to that covenant which you made with me by Moses, and broke in your rebellion against me in the days of Samuel, and in your election of another king.'

And in the New Testament, the angel Gabriel says of our Saviour (Luke 1:32–33): 'He shall be great, and be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord shall give him the throne of his father David; and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end.' This is also a kingdom on earth; for the claim of which, as an enemy to Caesar, he was put to death. The title of his cross was 'Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews'; he was crowned in scorn with a crown of thorns; and for the proclaiming of him it is said of the disciples (Acts 17:7) that 'they did all of them contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying there was another king, one Jesus.' The kingdom therefore of God is a real, not a metaphorical, kingdom — and so taken not only in the Old Testament but in the New. When we say, 'For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory,' it is to be understood of God's kingdom by force of our covenant, not by the right of God's power; for such a kingdom God always has. So it would be superfluous to say in our prayer, 'Your kingdom come,' unless it is meant of the restoration of that kingdom of God by Christ which by the revolt of the Israelites had been interrupted at the election of Saul. Nor would it have been proper to say 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand,' or to pray 'Your kingdom come,' if it had still continued.

There are so many other places that confirm this interpretation that it would be a wonder no greater notice is taken of it — except that it gives too much light to Christian kings to see their right of ecclesiastical government. This is what those have observed who, in place of 'sacerdotal kingdom,' translate 'a kingdom of priests'; for they may as well translate 'royal priesthood' (as it is in St Peter) into 'a priesthood of kings.' And whereas, for 'peculiar people,' they put 'precious jewel,' or 'treasure,' a man might as well call the special regiment, or company, of a general the general's 'precious jewel,' or his 'treasure.'

In short, the kingdom of God is a civil kingdom; which consisted first in the obligation of the people of Israel to those laws which Moses should bring to them from Mount Sinai, and which afterwards the high priest of the time being should deliver to them from before the cherubim in the Sanctum Sanctorum; and which kingdom, having been cast off at the election of Saul, the prophets foretold should be restored by Christ. And the restoration of it we daily pray for, when we say in the Lord's Prayer, 'Your kingdom come'; and the right of it we acknowledge, when we add, 'For yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, for ever and ever, amen'; and the proclaiming of it was the preaching of the apostles. To which men are prepared by the teachers of the gospel; to embrace which gospel (that is, to promise obedience to God's government) is to be in the kingdom of grace, because God has gratis given to such the power to be the subjects (that is, children) of God hereafter, when Christ shall come in majesty to judge the world, and actually to govern his own people — which is called the kingdom of glory. If the kingdom of God (also called the kingdom of heaven, from the gloriousness and admirable height of that throne) were not a kingdom which God, by his lieutenant or vicars, who deliver his commandments to the people, did exercise on earth, there would not have been so much contention and war about who it is by whom God speaks to us; nor would many priests have troubled themselves with spiritual jurisdiction, nor any king have denied it to them.

Out of this literal interpretation of the kingdom of God arises also the true interpretation of the word HOLY. For it is a word which in God's kingdom answers to that which men in their kingdoms use to call 'public,' or 'the king's.'

The king of any country is the public person, or representative, of all his own subjects. And God, the king of Israel, was the Holy One of Israel. The nation which is subject to one earthly sovereign is the nation of that sovereign — that is, of the public person. So the Jews, who were God's nation, were called (Exod. 19:6) 'a holy nation.' For by 'holy' is always understood either God himself, or what is God's in property; as by 'public' is always meant either the person of the commonwealth itself, or something that is so the commonwealth's that no private person can claim any property in it.

Therefore the Sabbath (God's day) is a holy day; the temple (God's house) a holy house; sacrifices, tithes, and offerings (God's tribute) holy duties; priests, prophets, and anointed kings under Christ (God's ministers) holy men; the celestial ministering spirits (God's messengers) holy angels; and the like. Wherever the word 'holy' is taken properly, there is always signified something of property, gotten by consent. In saying 'Hallowed be your name,' we do but pray to God for grace to keep the first commandment, of 'having no other gods but Him.' Mankind is God's nation in general, but the Jews only were a holy nation. Why? Because they became his property by covenant.

And the word 'profane' is usually taken in Scripture for the same as 'common'; and consequently their contraries, 'holy' and 'proper,' in the kingdom of God must be the same also. But figuratively, those men too are called holy who led such godly lives that it was as though they had forsaken all worldly designs, and wholly devoted, and given, themselves to God. In the proper sense, what is made holy by God's appropriating or separating it to his own use is said to be sanctified by God — as the seventh day in the fourth commandment; and as the elect in the New Testament were said to be sanctified when they were endowed with the spirit of godliness. And what is made holy by the dedication of men, and given to God so as to be used only in his public service, is also called SACRED, and said to be consecrated — as temples and other houses of public prayer, and their utensils, priests, and ministers, victims, offerings, and the external matter of the sacraments.

Of holiness there are degrees. For of those things set apart for the service of God, some may be set apart again, for a nearer and more especial service. The whole nation of the Israelites were a people holy to God; yet the tribe of Levi was, among the Israelites, a holy tribe; and among the Levites, the priests were yet more holy; and among the priests, the high priest was the most holy. So the land of Judea was the Holy Land; but the holy city in which God was to be worshipped was more holy; and again, the temple more holy than the city; and the Sanctum Sanctorum more holy than the rest of the temple.

A SACRAMENT is a setting apart of some visible thing from common use, and a consecration of it to God's service, for a sign — either of our admission into the kingdom of God, to be of the number of his peculiar people, or as a commemoration of the same. In the Old Testament, the sign of admission was circumcision; in the New Testament, baptism. The commemoration of it in the Old Testament was the eating (at a certain time, which was annual) of the paschal lamb, by which they were reminded of the night in which they were delivered out of their bondage in Egypt; and in the New Testament, the celebrating of the Lord's Supper, by which we are reminded of our deliverance from the bondage of sin, by our blessed Saviour's death on the cross. The sacraments of admission are to be used only once, because only one admission is needed; but because we have need of being often reminded of our deliverance, and of our allegiance, the sacraments of commemoration need to be repeated. These are the principal sacraments — as it were, the solemn oaths we make of our allegiance. There are also other consecrations that may be called sacraments, as the word implies only consecration to God's service; but as it implies an oath, or promise, of allegiance to God, there were no others in the Old Testament except circumcision and the Passover, nor are there any others in the New Testament except baptism and the Lord's Supper.
