title: Chapter 37. Of Miracles, and Their Use
paragraphs: By MIRACLES are signified the admirable works of God; and so they are also called wonders. And because they are for the most part done as a signification of his commandment — on such occasions as, without them, men are apt to doubt (following their private natural reasoning) what he has commanded and what he has not — they are commonly called in Holy Scripture signs, in the same sense as they are called by the Latins ostenta and portenta, from the showing and the foresignifying of what the Almighty is about to bring to pass.

To understand, then, what a miracle is, we must first understand what kinds of works men wonder at and call admirable. There are only two things that make men wonder at any event. One is, if it is strange — that is, such as the like has never, or very rarely, been produced. The other is, if when it is produced, we cannot imagine it to have been done by natural means, but only by the immediate hand of God. But when we see some possible natural cause of it, however rarely the like has been done, or if the like has often been done however impossible it may be to imagine a natural means for it, we no longer wonder, nor count it for a miracle.

So if a horse, or a cow, should speak, it would be a miracle, because the thing is strange and a natural cause is hard to imagine; so too would it be to see a strange deviation of nature in the production of some new shape of a living creature. But when a man, or other animal, begets his like, then, though we know no more of how this is done than of the other, since it is usual it is no miracle. In the same way, if a man is metamorphosed into a stone, or into a pillar, it is a miracle, because strange; but if a piece of wood is so changed, since we see it often, it is no miracle — and yet we know no more, by what operation of God the one is brought to pass than the other.

The first rainbow ever seen in the world was a miracle, because it was the first, and so strange, and served as a sign from God placed in heaven, to assure his people that there should be no more a universal destruction of the world by water. But today, because rainbows are frequent, they are not miracles, neither to those who know their natural causes, nor to those who do not. Again, there are many rare works produced by the art of man; yet when we know they are done — because by that we know also the means by which they are done — we do not count them for miracles, because they are not wrought by the immediate hand of God, but by the mediation of human industry.
What seems a miracle to one man may seem otherwise to another.

Furthermore, since admiration and wonder are consequent on the knowledge and experience with which men are endowed — some more, some less — it follows that the same thing may be a miracle to one and not to another. From this it comes that ignorant and superstitious men make great wonders of works that other men, knowing they proceed from nature (which is not the immediate, but the ordinary, work of God), do not admire at all: as when eclipses of the sun and moon have been taken for supernatural works by the common people, when nevertheless there were others who, from their natural causes, could have foretold the very hour at which they would happen. Or as when a man, by confederacy and secret intelligence, gets knowledge of the private actions of an ignorant, unwary man, and thereby tells him what he has done in former time — it seems to him a miraculous thing; but among wise, and cautious, men such miracles as these cannot easily be done.

Again, it belongs to the nature of a miracle that it be wrought to procure credit for God's messengers, ministers, and prophets — so that men may know they are called, sent, and employed by God, and thereby be the better inclined to obey them. And so, though the creation of the world, and afterwards the destruction of all living creatures in the universal deluge, were admirable works, they are not usually called miracles, because they were not done to procure credit for any prophet or other minister of God. For however admirable any work is, the admiration consists not in that it could be done — for men naturally believe the Almighty can do all things — but in that he does it at the prayer, or word, of a man. But the works of God in Egypt, by the hand of Moses, were properly miracles, because they were done with the intention of making the people of Israel believe that Moses came to them, not out of any design of his own interest, but as sent from God. So after God had commanded him to deliver the Israelites from the Egyptian bondage, when Moses said (Exod. 4:1 etc.), 'They will not believe me, but will say, The Lord has not appeared to me,' God gave him power to turn the rod he had in his hand into a serpent, and again to turn it back into a rod; and, by putting his hand into his bosom, to make it leprous, and again, by pulling it out, to make it whole — to make the children of Israel believe (as it is verse 5) that the God of their fathers had appeared to him. And if that were not enough, he gave him power to turn their waters into blood. And when he had done these miracles before the people, it is said (verse 41 [verse 31]) that 'they believed him.' Nevertheless, for fear of Pharaoh, they did not yet dare to obey him. So the other works which were done to plague Pharaoh and the Egyptians all tended to make the Israelites believe in Moses, and were properly miracles. In the same way, if we consider all the miracles done by the hand of Moses, and of all the rest of the prophets, until the captivity; and those of our Saviour, and his apostles afterwards — we shall find that their end was always to beget, or confirm, the belief that they did not come on their own motion, but were sent by God. We may further note in Scripture that the end of miracles was to beget belief, not universally in all men, elect and reprobate, but in the elect only — that is, in such as God had determined should become his subjects. For those miraculous plagues of Egypt did not have for their end the conversion of Pharaoh; for God had told Moses beforehand that he would harden the heart of Pharaoh, that he should not let the people go. And when at last he did let them go, it was not the miracles that persuaded him, but the plagues that forced him to it. So also of our Saviour it is written (Matt. 13:58) that he wrought not many miracles in his own country because of their unbelief; and (in Mark 6:5), instead of 'he wrought not many,' it is 'he could work none.' It was not that he lacked power — to say this would be blasphemy against God; nor that the end of miracles was not to convert incredulous men to Christ, for the end of all the miracles of Moses, of the prophets, of our Saviour, and of his apostles was to add men to the Church. It was because the end of their miracles was to add to the Church not all men, but such as should be saved — that is, such as God had elected. Since therefore our Saviour was sent from his Father, he could not use his power in the conversion of those whom his Father had rejected. Those who, expounding this passage of St Mark, say that his word 'he could not' is put for 'he would not,' do this without any example in the Greek tongue (where 'would not' is sometimes put for 'could not' in inanimate things which have no will, but 'could not' for 'would not' is never put), and so lay a stumbling-block before weak Christians, as if Christ could do no miracles except among the credulous.

From what I have set down here concerning the nature and use of a miracle, we may define it thus: 'A MIRACLE is a work of God (besides his operation by the way of nature, ordained in the creation) done for the making manifest to his elect of the mission of an extraordinary minister for their salvation.'

And from this definition we may infer, first, that in all miracles the work done is not the effect of any power in the prophet, because it is the effect of the immediate hand of God — that is, God has done it without using the prophet in it as a subordinate cause.

Second, that no devil, angel, or other created spirit can do a miracle. For it must be either by virtue of some natural science, or by incantation — that is, by virtue of words. For if the enchanters do it by their own power independent of God, there is some power that does not proceed from God, which all men deny; and if they do it by power given to them, then the work is not from the immediate hand of God, but natural — and consequently no miracle.

There are some texts of Scripture that seem to attribute the power of working wonders (equal to some of those immediate miracles wrought by God himself) to certain arts of magic, and incantation. For example, when we read that, after the rod of Moses, being cast on the ground, became a serpent, 'the magicians of Egypt did the like by their enchantments' (Exod. 7:11); and that after Moses had turned the waters of the Egyptian streams, rivers, ponds, and pools of water into blood, 'the magicians of Egypt did so likewise, with their enchantments' (Exod. 7:22); and that, after Moses had by the power of God brought frogs upon the land, 'the magicians also did so with their enchantments, and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt' (Exod. 8:7) — will not a man be apt to attribute miracles to enchantments — that is, to the efficacy of the sound of words — and think the same very well proved from this and other such passages? And yet there is no passage of Scripture that tells us what an enchantment is. So if enchantment is not, as many think it, the working of strange effects by spells and words, but imposture and delusion wrought by ordinary means — and so far from being supernatural that the impostors do not need so much as a study of natural causes, but only the ordinary ignorance, stupidity, and superstition of mankind to do them — then those texts that seem to countenance the power of magic, witchcraft, and enchantment must have a sense other than they seem at first sight to bear.

For it is plain enough that words have no effect except on those who understand them; and then they have no other effect but to signify the intentions or passions of those who speak, and thereby produce hope, fear, or other passions or conceptions in the hearer. So when a rod seems a serpent, or water blood, or any other miracle seems to be done by enchantment — if it is not for the edification of God's people — then neither the rod, nor the water, nor any other thing is enchanted, that is, wrought upon by the words; the spectator is. So all the miracle consists in this, that the enchanter has deceived a man — which is no miracle, but a very easy matter to do.

For such is the ignorance, and aptness to error, generally of all men — but especially of those who have little knowledge of natural causes, and of the nature and interests of men — that they may be misled by countless and easy tricks. What opinion of miraculous power, before it was known there is a science of the course of the stars, might a man have gained who told the people, 'At this hour, or day, the sun shall be darkened'? A juggler, by the handling of his cups and other trinkets, if it were not now commonly practised, would be thought to do his wonders at least by the power of the devil. A man who has practised to speak by drawing in his breath (which kind of men in ancient times were called ventriloqui), and so to make the weakness of his voice seem to proceed not from the weak impulsion of the organs of speech, but from distance of place, is able to make a great many men believe it is a voice from heaven, whatever he pleases to tell them. And for a cunning man who has inquired into the secrets and familiar confessions that one man ordinarily makes to another of his past actions and adventures, to tell them back to him is no hard matter; and yet there are many who by such means as this gain the reputation of being conjurers. But it would take too long to list all the various sorts of those men whom the Greeks called Thaumaturgi — that is, workers of wonderful things — and yet these do all they do by their own single dexterity. But if we look at the impostures wrought by confederacy, there is nothing, however impossible to be done, that is impossible to be believed. For two men conspiring, one to seem lame and the other to cure him with a charm, will deceive many; but many conspiring — one to seem lame, another so to cure him, and all the rest to bear witness — will deceive many more.

In this aptness of mankind to give too hasty belief to pretended miracles, there can be no better, nor (I think) any other, precaution than the one which God has prescribed, first by Moses (as I have said before in the previous chapter), at the beginning of Deuteronomy 13 and at the end of Deuteronomy 18: that we take none for prophets who teach any other religion than the one which God's lieutenant (who at that time was Moses) has established, nor any (even if he teaches the same religion) whose prediction we do not see come to pass. So Moses in his time, and Aaron and his successors in their times, and the sovereign governor of God's people, next under God himself — that is, the head of the church at all times — are to be consulted as to what doctrine he has established, before we give credit to a pretended miracle or prophet. And when that is done, the thing they claim to be a miracle we must both see done, and use all possible means to consider whether it is really done; and not only so, but whether it is such as no man can do the like by his natural power, but that it requires the immediate hand of God. And in this also we must have recourse to God's lieutenant, to whom in all doubtful cases we have submitted our private judgements. For example: if a man claims that after certain words spoken over a piece of bread, God has at once made it not bread, but a god, or a man, or both — and nevertheless it still looks as like bread as ever it did — there is no reason for any man to think it really done; nor, consequently, to fear him, till he inquires of God, by his vicar or lieutenant, whether it is done or not. If he says no, then follows what Moses says (Deut. 18:22): 'He has spoken it presumptuously; you shall not fear him.' If he says it is done, then he is not to be contradicted. So also if we do not see, but only hear tell of, a miracle, we are to consult the lawful church — that is, the lawful head of it — as to how far we are to give credit to those who report it. And this is chiefly the case of men who in these days live under Christian sovereigns. For in these times, I do not know of one man who ever saw any such wonderful work done by the charm, or at the word, or prayer of a man, that a man endowed with even a mediocrity of reason would think supernatural. And the question is no longer whether what we see done is a miracle, or whether the miracle we hear, or read of, was a real work and not the act of a tongue or a pen; but in plain terms, whether the report is true or a lie. In this question we are not each of us to make our own private reason, or conscience, the judge, but the public reason — that is, the reason of God's supreme lieutenant — is judge; and indeed we have made him judge already, if we have given him a sovereign power to do all that is necessary for our peace and defence. A private man has always the liberty (because thought is free) to believe, or not believe, in his heart those acts which have been given out for miracles, according as he shall see what benefit may come, by men's belief, to those who claim or countenance them, and thereby conjecture whether they are miracles or lies. But when it comes to the confession of that faith, the private reason must submit to the public — that is, to God's lieutenant. But who this lieutenant of God, and head of the church, is, shall be considered in its proper place hereafter.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 38. Of the Signification in Scripture of Eternal Life, Hell, Salvation, the World to Come, and Redemption
paragraphs: The maintenance of civil society depends on justice; and justice depends on the power of life and death, and on other lesser rewards and punishments, residing in those who have the sovereignty of the commonwealth. It is impossible that a commonwealth should stand where any other than the sovereign has the power of giving greater rewards than life, and of inflicting greater punishments than death. Now since eternal life is a greater reward than the present life, and eternal torment a greater punishment than the death of nature, it is a thing worth carefully considering — by all men who desire (by obeying authority) to avoid the calamities of confusion and civil war — what is meant in Holy Scripture by 'life eternal' and 'torment eternal'; and for what offences, and against whom committed, men are to be eternally tormented; and for what actions, they are to obtain eternal life.
The place of Adam's eternity, if he had not sinned: the terrestrial paradise.

And first we find that Adam was created in such a state of life that, had he not broken the commandment of God, he would have enjoyed it in the paradise of Eden everlastingly. For there was the tree of life, of which he was allowed to eat so long as he should forbear to eat of the tree of knowledge of good and evil — which was not allowed him. And so as soon as he had eaten of it, God thrust him out of paradise, 'lest he should put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever' (Gen. 3:22). By this it seems to me — with submission, nevertheless, both on this and on all questions whose determination depends on the Scriptures, to the interpretation of the Bible authorised by the commonwealth, whose subject I am — that Adam, had he not sinned, would have had an eternal life on earth, and that mortality entered upon himself and his posterity by his first sin. Not that actual death then entered: for Adam then could never have had children, whereas he lived long after, and saw a numerous posterity before he died. But where it is said, 'In the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die,' it must be meant of his mortality, and the certitude of death. Since then eternal life was lost by Adam's forfeiture, in committing sin, he who should cancel that forfeiture was to recover by that means the same life. Now Jesus Christ has satisfied for the sins of all who believe in him, and so has recovered to all believers that ETERNAL LIFE which was lost by the sin of Adam. And in this sense the comparison of St Paul holds (Rom. 5:18–19): 'As by the offence of one, judgement came on all men to condemnation, even so by the righteousness of one, the free gift came on all men to justification of life.' Which is again (1 Cor. 15:21–22) more clearly delivered in these words: 'For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.'

Concerning the place where men shall enjoy that eternal life which Christ has obtained for them, the texts just cited seem to make it on earth. For if, as in Adam all die — that is, have forfeited paradise and eternal life on earth — even so in Christ all shall be made alive, then all men shall be made to live on earth; for otherwise the comparison would not be proper. With this seems to agree the saying of the Psalmist (Ps. 133:3): 'Upon Zion God commanded the blessing, even life for evermore'; for Zion is in Jerusalem, on earth. As also the saying of St John (Rev. 2:7): 'To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.' This was the tree of Adam's eternal life; but his life was to have been on earth. The same seems to be confirmed again by St John (Rev. 21:2), where he says: 'I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband'; and again at verse 10, to the same effect — as if he should say, the new Jerusalem, the paradise of God, at the coming again of Christ, should come down to God's people from heaven, and not they go up to it from earth. And this differs not at all from what the two men in white clothing (that is, the two angels) said to the apostles, who were looking on Christ ascending (Acts 1:11): 'This same Jesus, who is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come, as you have seen him go up into heaven.' Which sounds as if they had said that he should come down to govern them under his Father, eternally, here — not take them up to govern them in heaven; and is in keeping with the restoration of the kingdom of God, instituted under Moses, which was a political government of the Jews on earth. Again, that saying of our Saviour (Matt. 22:30), 'that in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven,' is a description of an eternal life resembling what we lost in Adam, on the point of marriage. For since Adam and Eve, had they not sinned, would have lived on earth eternally in their individual persons, it is plain they should not have continually procreated their kind. For if immortals had generated as mankind does now, the earth in a small time would not be able to afford them a place to stand on. The Jews who asked our Saviour the question — whose wife the woman who had married many brothers should be in the resurrection — did not know the consequences of immortality: that there shall be no generation, and consequently no marriage, any more than there is marriage, or generation, among the angels. The comparison between that eternal life which Adam lost, and what our Saviour by his victory over death has recovered, holds also in this: that as Adam lost eternal life by his sin, and yet lived after it for a time, so the faithful Christian has recovered eternal life by Christ's passion, even though he dies a natural death, and remains dead for a time — namely, till the resurrection. For as death is reckoned from the condemnation of Adam, not from the execution; so life is reckoned from the absolution, not from the resurrection, of those who are elected in Christ.

That the place where men are to live eternally, after the resurrection, is the heavens — meaning by 'heaven' those parts of the world most remote from earth, where the stars are, or above the stars in another, higher, heaven called Caelum Empyreum (of which there is no mention in Scripture, nor ground in reason) — is not easily to be drawn from any text I can find. By 'the kingdom of heaven' is meant the kingdom of the king who dwells in heaven; and his kingdom was the people of Israel, whom he ruled by the prophets, his lieutenants — first Moses, and after him Eleazar, and the sovereign priests — until in the days of Samuel they rebelled and would have a mortal man for their king, after the manner of other nations. And when our Saviour Christ, by the preaching of his ministers, shall have persuaded the Jews to return, and called the Gentiles to his obedience, then shall there be a new kingdom of heaven, because our king shall then be God, whose throne is heaven — without any necessity evident in Scripture that man shall ascend to his happiness any higher than God's footstool, the earth. On the contrary, we find written (John 3:13) that 'no man has ascended into heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man, that is in heaven.' Where I observe in passing that these words are not, like those immediately before, the words of our Saviour, but of St John himself; for Christ was then not in heaven, but on the earth. The like is said of David (Acts 2:34), where St Peter, to prove the ascension of Christ, using the words of the Psalmist (Ps. 16:10), 'You will not leave my soul in hell, nor allow your Holy One to see corruption,' says they were spoken not of David, but of Christ; and to prove it, adds this reason: 'For David is not ascended into heaven.' But to this a man may easily answer, and say, that though their bodies were not to ascend until the general day of judgement, yet their souls were in heaven as soon as they were departed from their bodies. Which also seems to be confirmed by the words of our Saviour (Luke 20:37–38), who, proving the resurrection out of the word of Moses, says: 'That the dead are raised, even Moses showed at the bush, when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living, for they all live to him.' But if these words are to be understood only of the immortality of the soul, they do not prove at all what our Saviour intended to prove — which was the resurrection of the body, that is, the immortality of the man. So our Saviour means that those patriarchs were immortal, not by a property consequent on the essence and nature of mankind, but by the will of God, who was pleased of his mere grace to bestow eternal life on the faithful. And though at that time the patriarchs, and many other faithful men, were dead, yet, as it is in the text, they 'lived to God' — that is, they were written in the Book of Life with those who were absolved of their sins, and ordained to life eternal at the resurrection. That the soul of man is in its own nature eternal, and a living creature independent of the body — or that any mere man is immortal, otherwise than by the resurrection on the last day (except Enoch and Elijah) — is a doctrine not apparent in Scripture. The whole 14th chapter of Job, which is the speech not of his friends but of himself, is a complaint of this mortality of nature, and yet no contradiction of immortality at the resurrection. 'There is hope of a tree,' he says (verse 7), 'if it be cast down, that though the root of it grows old, and the stock of it dies in the ground, yet when it scents the water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. But man dies, and wastes away — yea, man gives up the ghost, and where is he?' And (verse 12), 'Man lies down, and rises not, till the heavens be no more.' But when is it that the heavens shall be no more? St Peter tells us it is at the general resurrection. For in his second Epistle, chapter 3, verse 7, he says, 'The heavens and the earth that are now are reserved to fire, against the day of judgement and perdition of ungodly men'; and (verse 12), 'looking for, and hastening to, the coming of God, in which the heavens shall be on fire, and shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat. Nevertheless, we, according to the promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, in which dwells righteousness.' So where Job says man does not rise till the heavens be no more, it is all one as if he had said, the immortal life (and 'soul' and 'life' in Scripture usually mean the same thing) does not begin in man until the resurrection and the day of judgement; and has for its cause not his specific nature and generation, but the promise. For St Peter does not say 'We look for new heavens and a new earth (from nature),' but 'from promise.'

Lastly, since it has already been proved out of various plain places of Scripture, in the 35th chapter of this book, that the kingdom of God is a civil commonwealth in which God himself is sovereign, by virtue first of the Old and then of the New Covenant, in which he reigns by his vicar or lieutenant — the same passages therefore also prove that, after the coming again of our Saviour in his majesty and glory, to reign actually and eternally, the kingdom of God is to be on earth. But because this doctrine (though proved from passages of Scripture neither few nor obscure) will seem to most men a novelty, I only put it forward, maintaining nothing in this, or in any other paradox of religion, but waiting for the end of that dispute of the sword concerning the authority (not yet decided among my countrymen) by which all kinds of doctrine are to be approved, or rejected; and whose commands, both in speech and in writing (whatever the opinions of private men may be), must be obeyed by all who mean to be protected by their laws. For the points of doctrine concerning the kingdom of God have so great an influence on the kingdom of man as not to be determined except by those who, under God, have the sovereign power.
The place after judgement of those who were never in the kingdom of God, or, having been in, are cast out.

As the kingdom of God, and eternal life, so also God's enemies and their torments after judgement appear by Scripture to have their place on earth. The name of the place where all men remain till the resurrection — those who were either buried, or swallowed up by the earth — is usually called in Scripture by words that signify 'under ground'; which the Latins generally read as Infernus and Inferni, and the Greeks Hades — that is, a place where men cannot see; and it includes the grave as well as any deeper place. But for the place of the damned after the resurrection, it is not determined either in the Old or in the New Testament by any note of location, but only by the company; as that it shall be where such wicked men were as God had in former times in an extraordinary and miraculous manner destroyed from off the face of the earth. As, for example, that they are in Inferno, in Tartarus, or in the bottomless pit, because Korah, Dathan, and Abiram were swallowed up alive into the earth. Not that the writers of Scripture would have us believe there could be in the globe of the earth — which is not only finite, but also (compared to the height of the stars) of no considerable size — a pit without a bottom, that is, a hole of infinite depth, such as the Greeks in their daemonology (their doctrine concerning daemons), and after them the Romans, called Tartarus; of which Virgil says:
Bis patet in praeceps, tantum tenditque sub umbras, / Quantus ad aethereum coeli suspectus Olympum.

For that is a thing the proportion of earth to heaven cannot bear. But rather that we should believe them to be there indefinitely — where those men are on whom God inflicted that exemplary punishment.

Again, because those mighty men of the earth who lived in the time of Noah, before the flood (which the Greeks called Heroes, and the Scripture Giants — and both say were begotten by the copulation of the children of God with the children of men), were destroyed for their wicked life by the general deluge, the place of the damned is therefore also sometimes marked out by the company of those deceased giants. As Proverbs 21:16: 'The man that wanders out of the way of understanding shall remain in the congregation of the giants.' And Job 26:5: 'Behold the giants groan under water, and they that dwell with them.' Here the place of the damned is under the water. And Isaiah 14:9: 'Hell is troubled how to meet you' (that is, the king of Babylon), 'and will displace the giants for you' — and here again the place of the damned (if the sense is literal) is to be under water.

Third, because the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, by the extraordinary wrath of God, were consumed for their wickedness with fire and brimstone, and together with them the country around them made a stinking bituminous lake, the place of the damned is sometimes expressed by fire, and a fiery lake. As in the Apocalypse 21:8: 'But the timorous, incredulous, and abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death.' So that it is plain that 'hellfire,' which is here expressed by metaphor from the real fire of Sodom, signifies no particular kind, or place, of torment, but is to be taken indefinitely for destruction — as it is in the 20th chapter, at the 14th verse, where it is said that 'death and hell were cast into the lake of fire' — that is, were abolished and destroyed; as if after the day of judgement there shall be no more dying, nor any more going into hell — that is, no more going to Hades (from which word our word 'hell' is perhaps derived), which is the same as no more dying.

Fourth, from the plague of darkness inflicted on the Egyptians, of which it is written (Exod. 10:23), 'They saw not one another, neither did any man rise from his place for three days; but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings,' the place of the wicked after judgement is called 'outer darkness' — or (as it is in the original) 'darkness without.' And so it is expressed (Matt. 22:13), where the king commands his servants 'to bind hand and foot the man that had not on his wedding garment, and to cast him out' — eis to skotos to exoteron, external darkness, or 'darkness without': which, though translated 'outer darkness,' does not signify how great, but where, that darkness is to be — namely, outside the habitation of God's elect.

Lastly, whereas there was a place near Jerusalem called the Valley of the Children of Hinnom — in a part of which, called Tophet, the Jews had committed most grievous idolatry, sacrificing their children to the idol Moloch; and in which also God had afflicted his enemies with most grievous punishments; and in which Josiah had burnt the priests of Moloch on their own altars, as appears at large in 2 Kings chapter 23 — that place served afterwards to receive the filth and garbage which was carried there out of the city; and there fires used to be made, from time to time, to purify the air and take away the stench of carrion. From this abominable place, the Jews used ever after to call the place of the damned by the name of Gehenna, or Valley of Hinnom. And this Gehenna is the word that is usually now translated HELL; and from the fires from time to time burning there, we get the notion of 'everlasting and unquenchable fire.'

Since now there is no one who so interprets the Scripture as that after the day of judgement the wicked are all eternally to be punished in the Valley of Hinnom; or that they shall so rise again as to be ever after under ground, or under water; or that after the resurrection they shall no more see one another, nor stir from one place to another — it follows, it seems to me, very necessarily that what is thus said concerning hellfire is spoken metaphorically; and that therefore there is a proper sense to be inquired after (for of all metaphors there is some real ground that may be expressed in proper words), both of the place of hell, and of the nature of hellish torment and tormentors.

And first, for the tormentors, we have their nature and properties exactly and properly delivered by the names of The Enemy, or Satan; The Accuser, or Diabolus; The Destroyer, or Abaddon. Which significant names — Satan, Devil, Abaddon — set forth to us no individual person, as proper names usually do, but only an office, or quality; and are therefore appellatives, which ought not to have been left untranslated, as they are, in the Latin and modern Bibles. For thereby they seem to be the proper names of daemons; and men are the more easily seduced to believe the doctrine of devils — which at that time was the religion of the Gentiles, and contrary to that of Moses, and of Christ.

And because by the Enemy, the Accuser, and the Destroyer is meant the enemy of those who shall be in the kingdom of God, therefore if the kingdom of God after the resurrection is on earth (as in the previous chapter I have shown by Scripture it seems to be), the Enemy, and his kingdom, must be on earth also. For so it was in the time before the Jews had deposed God. For God's kingdom was in Palestine, and the nations round about were the kingdoms of the Enemy; and consequently by 'Satan' is meant any earthly enemy of the church.

The torments of hell are expressed sometimes by 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' (as Matt. 8:12); sometimes by 'the worm of conscience' (as Isa. 66:24 and Mark 9:44, 46, 48); sometimes by fire, as in the place now quoted, 'where the worm dies not, and the fire is not quenched,' and in many other places besides; sometimes by 'shame and contempt,' as Dan. 12:2: 'And many of those that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake; some to everlasting life, and some to shame, and everlasting contempt.' All these places designate metaphorically a grief and discontent of mind, from the sight of that eternal felicity in others which they themselves through their own incredulity and disobedience have lost. And because such felicity in others is not perceptible except by comparison with their own actual miseries, it follows that they are to suffer such bodily pains and calamities as are incident to those who not only live under evil and cruel governors, but also have for their enemy the eternal king of the saints, God Almighty. And among these bodily pains is to be reckoned also, for every one of the wicked, a second death. For though the Scripture is clear for a universal resurrection, we do not read that to any of the reprobate an eternal life is promised. For whereas St Paul (1 Cor. 15:42–43), to the question of what bodies men shall rise with again, says that 'the body is sown in corruption, and is raised in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory; it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power' — glory and power cannot be applied to the bodies of the wicked. Nor can the name of 'second death' be applied to those who can never die but once; and although in metaphorical speech a calamitous everlasting life may be called an everlasting death, it cannot well be understood of a second death. The fire prepared for the wicked is an everlasting fire — that is, the state in which no man can be without torture, both of body and of mind, after the resurrection, shall endure for ever; and in that sense the fire shall be unquenchable, and the torments everlasting. But it cannot from this be inferred that he who shall be cast into that fire, or tormented with those torments, shall endure and resist them so as to be eternally burnt and tortured and yet never destroyed, nor die. And though there are many places that affirm everlasting fire and torments (into which men may be cast successively, one after another, forever), I find none that affirm there shall be an eternal life therein of any individual person; but on the contrary, an everlasting death — which is the second death (Apocalypse 20:13–14): 'For after death and the grave shall have delivered up the dead which were in them, and every man be judged according to his works; death and the grave shall also be cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.' Whereby it is plain that there is to be a second death of every one who shall be condemned at the day of judgement, after which he shall die no more.
The joys of life eternal and salvation are the same thing; salvation from sin, and from misery, are all one.

The joys of life eternal are in Scripture all comprehended under the name of SALVATION, or being saved. To be saved is to be made secure — either relatively, against particular evils, or absolutely, against all evil (including want, sickness, and death itself). And because man was created in an immortal condition, not subject to corruption, and consequently to nothing tending to the dissolution of his nature, and fell from that happiness by the sin of Adam, it follows that to be saved from sin is to be saved from all the evil and calamities that sin has brought upon us. And so in Holy Scripture, remission of sin, and salvation from death and misery, are the same thing — as appears from the words of our Saviour, who, having cured a man sick of the palsy by saying (Matt. 9:2), 'Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you,' and knowing that the scribes took it for blasphemy that a man should claim to forgive sins, asked them (verse 5) 'whether it were easier to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or, Arise and walk' — signifying that it was all one, as to the saving of the sick man, to say 'Your sins are forgiven' and 'Arise and walk'; and that he used that form of speech only to show he had power to forgive sins. And it is besides evident in reason that, since death and misery were the punishments of sin, the discharge of sin must also be a discharge of death and misery — that is, salvation absolute, such as the faithful are to enjoy after the day of judgement, by the power, and favour, of Jesus Christ, who for that cause is called our SAVIOUR.

Concerning particular salvations, such as are meant in 1 Sam. 14:39 — 'as the Lord lives, that saves Israel' (that is, from their temporary enemies); and 2 Sam. 22:4, 'You are my saviour; you save me from violence'; and 2 Kings 13:5, 'God gave the Israelites a saviour, and so they were delivered from the hand of the Assyrians'; and the like — I need say nothing, since there is neither difficulty nor interest to corrupt the interpretation of texts of that kind.

But concerning general salvation, because it must be in the kingdom of heaven, there is great difficulty concerning the place. On one hand, by 'kingdom' (which is an estate ordained by men for their perpetual security against enemies, and against want), it seems that this salvation should be on earth. For by salvation is set out to us a glorious reign of our king by conquest — not a safety by escape; and therefore where we look for salvation, we must look also for triumph; and before triumph, for victory; and before victory, for battle — which cannot well be supposed to be in heaven. But however good this reason may be, I will not trust to it without very plain passages of Scripture. The state of salvation is described at length in Isaiah 33:20–24:

'Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnities; your eyes shall see Jerusalem a quiet habitation, a tabernacle that shall not be taken down; not one of its stakes shall ever be removed, neither shall any of its cords be broken.
But there the glorious Lord will be to us a place of broad rivers, and streams, in which shall go no galley with oars, neither shall a gallant ship pass by.
For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he will save us.
Your tacklings are loosed; they could not well strengthen their mast; they could not spread the sail; then is the prey of a great spoil divided; the lame take the prey.
And the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick; the people that shall dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity.'

In these words we have the place from which salvation is to proceed: 'Jerusalem, a quiet habitation'; the eternity of it: 'a tabernacle that shall not be taken down,' etc.; the Saviour of it: 'the Lord, their judge, their lawgiver, their king; he will save us'; the salvation: 'the Lord shall be to them as a broad moat of swift waters,' etc.; the condition of their enemies: 'their tacklings are loose, their masts weak; the lame shall take the spoil of them'; the condition of the saved: 'the inhabitants shall not say, I am sick'; and lastly, all this is comprehended in forgiveness of sin: 'the people that dwell therein shall be forgiven their iniquity.' By which it is plain that salvation shall be on earth, then, when God shall reign (at the coming again of Christ) in Jerusalem; and from Jerusalem shall proceed the salvation of the Gentiles, who shall be received into God's kingdom. As is also more expressly declared by the same prophet, chapter 66:20–21: 'And they' (that is, the Gentiles who had any Jew in bondage) 'shall bring all your brethren, for an offering to the Lord, out of all nations, on horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and on mules, and on swift beasts, to my holy mountain, Jerusalem, says the Lord, as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord. And I will also take of them for priests and for Levites, says the Lord.' Whereby it is plain that the chief seat of God's kingdom (which is the place from which the salvation of us who were Gentiles shall proceed) shall be Jerusalem. And the same is also confirmed by our Saviour, in his discourse with the woman of Samaria, concerning the place of God's worship; to whom he says (John 4:22) that the Samaritans worshipped they knew not what, but the Jews worshipped what they knew, 'For salvation is of the Jews' (Ex Judais, that is, begins with the Jews) — as if he should say, you worship God, but do not know by whom he will save you, as we do, who know it shall be one of the tribe of Judah, a Jew, not a Samaritan. And so also the woman not impertinently answered him again: 'We know the Messiah shall come.' So what our Saviour says, 'Salvation is from the Jews,' is the same as Paul says (Rom. 1:16–17): 'The gospel is the power of God to salvation to every one that believes — to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. For in it is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith' — from the faith of the Jew, to the faith of the Gentile. In the like sense the prophet Joel, describing the day of judgement (chapter 2:30–31), says that God would 'show wonders in heaven and in earth, blood, and fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord come,' and adds (verse 32), 'and it shall come to pass, that whoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. For in Mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, shall be salvation.' And Obadiah verse 17 says the same: 'Upon Mount Zion shall be deliverance; and there shall be holiness, and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions' — that is, the possessions of the heathen, which he expresses more particularly in the following verses, by the Mount of Esau, the land of the Philistines, the fields of Ephraim, of Samaria, Gilead, and the cities of the south; and concludes with these words: 'The kingdom shall be the Lord's.' All these passages are for salvation, and the kingdom of God (after the day of judgement) upon earth. On the other hand, I have not found any text that can probably be drawn to prove any ascension of the saints into heaven — that is, into any Caelum Empyreum or other ethereal region — except that it is called the kingdom of heaven. Which name it may have because God, who was king of the Jews, governed them by his commands sent to Moses by angels from heaven, to reduce them to their obedience; and shall send him from there again, to rule both them and all other faithful men, from the day of judgement, everlastingly; or from this, that the throne of this our great king is in heaven, whereas the earth is only his footstool. But that the subjects of God should have any place as high as his throne, or higher than his footstool, seems not suitable to the dignity of a king; nor can I find any plain text for it in Holy Scripture.

From what has been said of the kingdom of God, and of salvation, it is not hard to interpret what is meant by the WORLD TO COME. Three worlds are mentioned in Scripture: the Old World, the Present World, and the World to Come. Of the first, St Peter speaks (2 Pet. 2:5): 'If God spared not the old world, but saved Noah, the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing the flood upon the world of the ungodly,' and so on. So the first world was from Adam to the general flood. Of the present world, our Saviour speaks (John 18:36): 'My kingdom is not of this world.' For he came only to teach men the way of salvation, and to renew the kingdom of his Father by his doctrine. Of the world to come, St Peter speaks (2 Pet. 3:13): 'Nevertheless, according to his promise, we look for new heavens, and a new earth.' This is that WORLD in which Christ, coming down from heaven, in the clouds, with great power and glory, shall send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, and from the uttermost parts of the earth, and thenceforth reign over them (under his Father) everlastingly.

The salvation of a sinner supposes a previous REDEMPTION; for he who is once guilty of sin is liable to the penalty of it, and must pay (or some other for him) such ransom as he who is offended, and has him in his power, shall require. And since the person offended is Almighty God, in whose power are all things, such ransom is to be paid before salvation can be acquired as God has been pleased to require. By this ransom is not meant a satisfaction for sin equivalent to the offence — which no sinner for himself, nor righteous man, can ever be able to make for another. The damage a man does to another, he may make amends for by restitution, or recompense; but sin cannot be taken away by recompense, for that would be to make the liberty to sin a thing vendible. But sins may be pardoned to the repentant, either gratis, or on such penalty as God is pleased to accept. What God usually accepted in the Old Testament was some sacrifice, or oblation. To forgive sin is not an act of injustice, even though the punishment has been threatened. Even among men, though the promise of good binds the promiser, threats — that is, promises of evil — do not bind them; much less shall they bind God, who is infinitely more merciful than men. Our Saviour Christ therefore, to redeem us, did not, in the sense in which his death by its own power could make it unjust in God to punish sinners with eternal death, satisfy for the sins of men; but he did make that sacrifice and oblation of himself, at his first coming, which God was pleased to require, for the salvation at his second coming of such as in the meantime should repent and believe in him. And though this act of our redemption is not always in Scripture called a sacrifice and oblation, but sometimes a price, yet by 'price' we are not to understand anything by the value of which he could claim right to a pardon for us from his offended Father, but the price which God the Father was pleased in mercy to demand.
section: Part III — Of a Christian Commonwealth

title: Chapter 39. Of the Signification in Scripture of the Word Church
paragraphs: The word 'Church' (Ecclesia) signifies in the books of Holy Scripture various things. Sometimes (though not often) it is taken for God's house — that is, for a temple in which Christians assemble to perform holy duties publicly. As in 1 Cor. 14:34: 'Let your women keep silence in the churches.' But this is put metaphorically for the congregation assembled there; and the word has since been used for the building itself, to distinguish the temples of Christians from those of idolaters. The temple of Jerusalem was God's house and the house of prayer; and so is any building dedicated by Christians to the worship of Christ Christ's house — and therefore the Greek fathers call it Kuriake, the Lord's house; and from there, in our language it came to be called Kyrke, and Church.

Church (when not taken for a building) signifies the same as Ecclesia signified in the Grecian commonwealths — that is, a congregation, or assembly, of citizens called forth to hear the magistrate speak to them, and which in the Roman commonwealth was called concio (as the one who spoke was called ecclesiastes, and concionator). When they were called forth by lawful authority (Acts 19:39), it was Ecclesia Legitima, a lawful church, ennomos ekklesia. But when they were stirred up by tumultuous and seditious clamour, it was a confused church, ekklesia sygkechumene.

It is also taken sometimes for the men who have the right to be of the congregation, though not actually assembled — that is, for the whole multitude of Christian men, however far dispersed: as in Acts 8:3, where it is said that 'Saul made havoc of the church.' And in this sense Christ is said to be head of the church. And sometimes for a certain part of Christians, as in Col. 4:15, 'Salute the church that is in his house.' Sometimes also for the elect only, as in Eph. 5:27, 'A glorious church, without spot, or wrinkle, holy and without blemish' — which is meant of the church triumphant, or church to come. Sometimes for a congregation, assembled, of professors of Christianity — whether their profession be true, or counterfeit — as it is meant in Matt. 18:17, where it is said, 'Tell it to the church; and if he neglects to hear the church, let him be to you as a Gentile, or a publican.'

And it is in this last sense only that the church can be taken for one person — that is, can be said to have power to will, to pronounce, to command, to be obeyed, to make laws, or to do any other action whatever. For without authority from a lawful congregation, whatever act is done in a gathering of people is the particular act of every one of those who were present, and gave their aid in performing it; and not the act of all of them in bulk, as of one body — much less the act of those who were absent, or who, being present, were not willing it should be done. According to this sense, I define a CHURCH as 'a company of men professing the Christian religion, united in the person of one sovereign, at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.' And because in all commonwealths an assembly without warrant from the civil sovereign is unlawful, that church too, which is assembled in any commonwealth that has forbidden them to assemble, is an unlawful assembly.

It also follows that there is on earth no such universal church to which all Christians are bound to obey, because there is no power on earth to which all other commonwealths are subject. There are Christians in the dominions of various princes and states; but every one of them is subject to that commonwealth of which he is himself a member, and consequently cannot be subject to the commands of any other person. And so a church such as is capable of commanding, judging, absolving, condemning, or doing any other act, is the same thing as a civil commonwealth consisting of Christian men, and is called a civil state because its subjects are men, and a church because its subjects are Christians. 'Temporal' and 'spiritual' government are only two words brought into the world to make men see double, and mistake their lawful sovereign. It is true that the bodies of the faithful, after the resurrection, shall be not only spiritual but eternal; but in this life they are gross, and corruptible. There is therefore no other government in this life, neither of state nor of religion, but temporal; nor any teaching of any doctrine lawful to any subject which the governor both of the state and of religion forbids to be taught. And that governor must be one, or else there must inevitably follow faction and civil war in the commonwealth, between the church and the state, between spiritualists and temporalists, between the sword of justice and the shield of faith — and (what is more) in every Christian man's own breast, between the Christian and the man. The doctors of the church are called pastors; so also are civil sovereigns. But if pastors are not subordinate one to another, so that there may be one chief pastor, men will be taught contrary doctrines, of which both may be — and one must be — false. Who that one chief pastor is, according to the law of nature, has already been shown: namely, that it is the civil sovereign. And to whom Scripture has assigned that office, we shall see in the following chapters.
